Supreme Court grapples over whether Colorado can exclude religious schools from pre-K funding for opposing gay marriage
See more of our coverage in your search results.
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court’s conservative justices signaled Tuesday they may side with Catholic preschools who refused to sign a pledge to welcome students whose parents are transgender or gay.
At issue is whether a state may, without ever naming religion, attach a condition to public money in Colorado’s taxpayer-funded universal preschool program it knows certain faiths cannot accept.
Colorado launched its Universal Preschool Program in 2023, providing 15 hours per week of tuition-free preschool to every 4-year-old in the Centennial State.
The program is open to public, private, and religious schools as long as they sign a nondiscrimination pact agreeing that a child or parent’s sexual orientation or gender identity won’t impact their enrollment.
Justices Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett all pressed Colorado’s conditions, while Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson warned that the parishes were asking for a special exemption that no secular school enjoys.
Chief Justice John Roberts, who could hold the deciding vote, pressed both sides.
Roberts opened by noting that the court’s last three rulings for religious schools each struck down laws that singled out a religion by name; Colorado’s does not.
“I’m not quite sure how you limit the applicability of your principle,” he told Nicholas Reaves, the lawyer for the parishes, asking whether it would apply to driver’s licenses, employment benefits and Social Security.
“It seems to me that you’re quite anxious to bury Sherbert,” Roberts later told Colorado’s lawyer, Helen Norton, “perhaps as anxious as the other side is to bury Smith.”
The heart of the dispute lies between those two cases. Sherbert v. Verner, decided in 1963, barred the government from denying benefits over a person’s religious practice — unless it could survive strict scrutiny, the highest legal standard the government must meet to defend a law or policy. Employment Division v. Smith, decided in 1990, cut the other way, holding that a law that applies to everyone generally stands, however heavily it falls on a particular creed.
The parishes had also asked the justices to overturn Smith outright, but the court refused to take up that question. Alito, who has urged the court to toss the precedent in the past, said Tuesday he would not argue for overruling it “here today.”
Gorsuch suggested Colorado had found a backdoor around the court’s recent rulings for religious schools.
“The Constitution tends to deal in substances, not in shadows and procedures,” he said.
Kavanaugh noted that Colorado lets participating preschools set enrollment preferences for a range of secular reasons.
“You can have a vegetarian school, but you can’t have a Catholic school,” he said.
Barrett questioned what problem the rule was supposed to solve.
“It’s just hard for me to imagine that this kind of discrimination is a problem in Colorado and that you could be responding to anything else other than the religious schools,” she said.
Sotomayor pressed Reaves to say plainly whether the schools would reject a child “merely because their parents are homosexual.”
“I would say if it’s the sincere religious exercise of the petitioner, then I think it would be permitted,” Reaves answered.
Sotomayor then asked whether the same principle would let a school exclude black children. Reaves said no.
The schools do not automatically reject the children of gay couples, Reaves told the justices, though enrollment might be refused in some cases.
“The principle at issue here is, do you have to treat them better?” Kagan said.
Jackson pressed the DOJ’s lawyer, Sarah Harris, on the same line, arguing there was “no principled basis” to distinguish a religious objection to gay parents from one to black parents. Harris said a racial exclusion would likely fail strict scrutiny.
Norton told the justices that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools” and that the state’s aim was “equal opportunity, not some opportunity.”
The Trump administration sided with the parishes. Harris called the court’s religious liberty precedents a “Swiss cheese doctrinal setup” and urged the justices to restore stricter protections for believers in public benefit programs.
St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, St. Bernadette Catholic Parish in Lakewood, the Archdiocese of Denver and Daniel and Lisa Sheley, Catholic parents who want to use the funding at a parish preschool, sued in 2023 after the state rejected the archdiocese’s request for a religious exemption.
The archdiocese, which runs 34 preschools, wants its schools to be able to admit only families who agree to uphold Catholic beliefs on sex and gender — a policy Colorado says would let them turn away children because of their own or their parents’ sexual orientation or transgender status.

The parishes sued, arguing the requirement violates the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause because Colorado grants exceptions to some providers — including for placing children with disabilities — while refusing to accommodate religious schools.
The lower courts rejected the push by the plaintiffs for a permanent injunction against Colorado’s requirement that schools sign the nondiscrimination pact.
Since 2018, Colorado’s LGBT protections have come before the Supreme Court three times on religious or free speech challenges. The state lost all three.
In March, the justices ruled 8-1 that the state’s ban on conversion therapy for minors, as applied ot a Christian counselor’s talk therapy, regulates speech by viewpoint. They sent the case back for stricter review.
In 2023, the high court ruled against Colorado for trying to force a web designer to create websites for same-sex couples.
Perhaps most famously, the court in 2018 backed a baker in Colorado who refused to bake a customized cake for a gay wedding due to his religious beliefs.
Reaves closed by noting that the Sheleys, the Catholic parents in the case, are short $18,000 because of the policy.
A decision in the St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy case is expected by the end of June.

sources.news_title: ‘Not a zero sum game’: Supreme Court hears contentious arguments on religious freedom fight over preschool program * WorldNetDaily * by Fred Lucas, The Daily Signal
sources.text:
The Supreme Court could deliver another blow to Colorado in a religious liberty case over the state’s exclusion of a Catholic church from a “universal” preschool program.
Justices heard oral arguments in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy on Tuesday.
“This is not a zero sum game. Letting families use universal preschool funding at Catholic schools won’t take away a single seat from the over 2,000 preschools already participating in the program,” argued the plaintiffs’ attorney Nicholas Reaves before the court. “In fact, letting Catholic schools in will create more seats for everyone even for families who disagree with Catholic teachings.”
Colorado’s actions were at the center of religious freedom disputes before the high court in 2018, 2023, and earlier this year, losing each case.
In this case, the state’s program provides all children with up to 15 hours of tuition-free preschool, but it requires participating schools to admit LGBTQ-identifying children and the children of LGBTQ-identifying parents.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor, a liberal justice, became animated at several points during her questioning, asserting that the “bottom line” was “Your Catholic schools will reject the child merely because their parents are homosexual.”
Reaves disagreed.
“If the government is excluding someone from a public benefit solely on account of their religious exercise, that would trigger strict scrutiny,” Reaves said. “The government would have to come forward and say, ‘we have a really good reason for this.’ And we just don’t think they’ve done that in this case.”
Justice Brett Kavanaugh later addressed the Sotomayor question, asking, “You don’t categorically exclude children of those in same-sex marriages.”
Reaves replied, “Correct.”
Helen Norton, arguing for Colorado, argued that the universal pre-K program, referred to as UPK, does not discriminate on the basis of religion, but Justice Amy Coney Barrett pressed her on the issue.
“You agree, don’t you, that Colorado could not say that Catholic schools or Evangelical schools or Orthodox Jewish schools were excluded from participation in the UPK program,” Barrett asked.
“Absolutely. They’re welcome,” Norton replied.
Barrett followed, “Then explain what the differences between that and then choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools will be unable to agree to.”
Norton replied, “There’s no evidence of any animus hostility in this case.”
Barrett replied, “I’m not assuming animus against religion. But if you know that the effect of choosing that requirement will push out those of a contrary belief, how is that different?”
Norton replied that the state even convened a working group of faith-based providers that included St. Mary to solicit their input and welcome their inclusion in the program.
“It’s absolutely true that states engage in religious discrimination and triggers trick scrutiny when they have the intent to disfavor religion, regardless of whether that intent is transparent or hidden. Here, there is zero evidence of Colorado’s intent.”
St. Mary’s Catholic Parish preschool in Littleton, Colorado, has argued its exclusion from the state’s universal preschool program violates the First Amendment’s protection against religious discrimination.
The plaintiffs in the case are two Catholic parishes, two Catholic parents, and the Catholic Archdiocese of Denver. The defendant is Lisa Roy, executive director of the Colorado Department of Early Childhood.
A district court and the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Colorado, citing the Supreme Court’s 1990 decision in Employment Division v. Smith that the state’s rules were neutral and applied to every preschool without distinction.
In the 1990 precedent, the Supreme Court allowed Oregon to exclude a Native American man from receiving unemployment benefits because he had consumed the hallucinogen peyote, which he claimed was part of his religious practice. Congress then passed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993, which requires strict scrutiny for laws restricting religious freedom.
Plaintiffs also note that two federal appeals courts and two state supreme courts have ruled differently from the 10th Circuit on the same question.
The state has argued in its response that the parish seeks “an exemption from this law to allow them to receive public funding while turning away preschoolers because of their, or their parents’ gender identity or sexual orientation.”
This could mark another setback for Colorado in religious freedom cases.
In March, the Supreme Court held that Colorado’s ban on talk therapy for minors regarding gender identity or sexual orientation violated the First Amendment because it imposed a viewpoint-based restriction on speech.
In 2023 and 2018, the high court held that Colorado could not compel a Christian website designer and a Christian baker, respectively, to provide specific creative services for same-sex weddings.
[Editor’s note: This story originally was published by The Daily Signal.]

Supreme Court considers whether a state's preschool funding rules are discriminatory
sources.text:
Supreme Court considers whether a state’s preschool funding rules are discriminatory
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Colorado denied public funds to Catholic preschools that excluded same-sex parents and their children.
- The court’s six conservatives leaned in favor of ruling the state was discriminating based on religion.
WASHINGTON — In its latest chapter on religion in schools, the Supreme Court debated Tuesday whether Colorado may fund private preschools for 4-year-olds but exclude Catholic schools that refuse to serve same-sex parents and their children.
The court’s six conservatives, all of whom were raised Catholic, leaned in favor of ruling the state was discriminating based on religion.
The state offered funding to all preschools but said they must abide by an “equal opportunity” rule that forbids discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett said state officials “chose to impose a condition” they knew those Catholic schools “will be unable to agree to.”
In contrast, the court’s three liberals said the Catholic schools were not seeking equal treatment but a new right to discriminate.
“You are asking for a special rule for religious schools,” said Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor said the state opened the funding program to all schools, including church-related schools. “The Catholic schools are not being excluded. They’re choosing not to participate because they won’t get an exemption,” she said.
In the last decade, the court’s conservative majority has strengthened the 1st Amendment’s protection for the “free exercise of religion.”
The right to possess an AR-15 is just one of nearly 60 cases the court will hear in the new term.
States and local governments need not offer public funds to private groups and entities, the justices said. But if they do so, they may not single out religious schools or people and deny them public funding that is open to all.
They struck down laws in Minnesota and Maine that denied scholarships or school funds to students who enrolled in a religious school. And they ruled the city of Philadelphia could not bar Catholic social services from providing foster care because they did not work with same-sex couples.
Despite that history, Colorado adopted a strong “equal opportunity” law in 2022 to go with its new state funding for preschools.
The state voters had approved a ballot measure in 2020 to provide public funding for a year of preschool prior to kindergarten. Both public and private schools were encouraged to participate.
The state pays for 15 hours per week and provides parents about $6,000 in tuition.
Lawmakers said eligible schools must provide children “an equal opportunity to enroll regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level or disability.”
The Archdiocese of Denver oversees 34 Catholic preschools. Parents were told they must support and affirm the teachings of the church, including on matters of gender and marriage.
In light of the new funding law, the church asked for an accommodation that would allow “faith based providers to participate in the program without compromising their sincerely held religious beliefs.”
The state refused. It said “no provider may discriminate against children or families in violation of the state statute.”
St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colo., and two of its parents sued, alleging a violation of the 1st Amendment.
Their attorneys — the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty — argued that no LGBTQ+ family has been harmed or claimed discrimination under the preschool funding law, while “thousands of Catholic families have zero Catholic preschools available to them.”
They lost before a federal judge and the 10th Circuit Court. Those judges said the state did not target the Catholic schools or treat them differently from others because of their religious beliefs.
The Supreme Court agreed in April to hear the case of St. Mary Catholic Parish vs. Roy.
During Tuesday’s argument, Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh voiced dismay over how this case arose.
“This seems like a would-be solution in search of a problem. Why are we here?” he asked a state attorney.
He and Barrett said same-sex couples did not seek to have their children enrolled in Catholic preschools. Meanwhile, other parents were denied state funds because of the marriage and family policies of the Catholic parishes.
The court is likely to hand down a decision in several months.

sources.news_title: Can This Religious Preschool Exclude LGBTQ Families and Still Get State Funding?
sources.text:
A majority of U.S. Supreme Court justices on Tuesday appeared inclined to require Colorado to allow Catholic preschools to participate in the state’s universal prekindergarten program without signing an anti-discrimination pledge that covers sexual orientation and gender identity.
The case of St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy holds implications well beyond preschool. The court seems likely to continue a line of recent decisions that have allowed religious schools to participate in school choice programs. It will also answer whether private religious schools participating in such programs must allow families with same-sex parents or gay or transgender children. And a decision for the Catholic Church here could be felt in the public schools.
“Is the next case parents in a public school saying it’s really important to my religious beliefs that my child not be educated with children of same-sex parents?” Justice Elena Kagan asked during the two-hour argument.
But several of the court’s more conservative members appeared more sympathetic to the challengers of the anti-discrimination requirement, who argue that it runs counter to church teachings on sexuality and same-sex marriage.
Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. said, “We have here a requirement that has a very severe impact on certain religions, and that was something that everybody could have anticipated. And we have little evidence of a practical problem—little evidence, if any evidence … that there are LGBTQ couples who cannot find other preschools to send their children to.”
Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh said there was a “clash of rights” between the free exercise concerns of religious adherents and the right to same-sex marriage recognized by the Supreme Court.
“There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 [pre]schools [an] appropriate fit for their children, which could, in fact, be at one of the Catholic preschools, depending on their own beliefs about that, and you avoid the clash,” he said. “I’m just trying to figure out why we’re here.”
A state’s major expansion of pre-K
The Colorado case involves a 2020 ballot measure establishing a universal pre-K program, which offers every 4-year-old in the state up to 15 hours of free preschool per week.
Colorado’s pre-K program is open to public, private, and religious providers alike, but all must sign an agreement to adhere to the state’s quality standards, which include a nondiscrimination requirement that covers, among other things, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, and gender identity.
“Colorado welcomes religious preschools to [universal pre-K],” said Helen Norton, Colorado’s deputy solicitor general. “The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike.”
And under the program, “faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage,” Norton said. But they must be open to all, regardless of whether the students’ parents are in a same-sex union.
The Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Denver, which oversees 34 Catholic preschools, believes the equal-opportunity mandate interferes with Catholic teaching on sexual orientation and gender identity.
“The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation,” said Nicholas R. Reaves of the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, the organization representing the Catholic challengers. “To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the church’s teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the state has denied Colorado families the ability to use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools.”
The Denver Archdiocese and other faith-based preschool providers sought a religious exemption from the nondiscrimination requirement, but the Colorado Department of Early Childhood said no.
“I cannot grant an accommodation to a nondiscrimination … statement that’s in statute,” Lisa Roy, the department’s executive director, testified in a 2023 deposition.
The state’s refusal to provide an exemption was challenged under the First Amendment’s free exercise of religion clause by St. Mary and one other church in the archdiocese, as well as one family in the parish that says it missed out on some $12,000 in state pre-K aid because St. Mary could not participate in the state program.
The St. Mary case is a followup to three recent cases in which the Supreme Court expanded its approach to government aid flowing to religious schools. The court’s 2017 ruling in Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia v. Comer, its 2020 decision in Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, and its 2022 ruling in Carson v. Makin all overturned state exclusions of religious schools from generally available aid programs such as playground grants, scholarship tax credits, and tuition aid.
The most recent of those, Carson, said the state of Maine’s exclusion of religious schools from a program providing state aid for tuition covering students from towns without public high schools failed strict scrutiny under the free exercise clause.
The lawsuit argues that Colorado’s equal-opportunity mandate violated the Carson decision by excluding the Catholic schools from the pre-K program based solely on their religious character and exercise.
But two lower federal courts applied Employment Division v. Smith, the 1990 Supreme Court decision that says the free exercise clause cannot exempt individuals from neutral, generally applicable laws. The courts held that the pre-K program’s nondiscrimination requirements met that standard.
‘A special rule’ for faith-based schools?
In addition to Kagan, the court’s two other most liberal members also appeared supportive of Colorado.
“When Colorado says anyone who receives these funds has to be open to everyone and can’t discriminate, what you’re asking for in the context of this free exercise claim is a special rule for religious schools to be able to not follow that condition,” Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told Reaves.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor told Reaves, “Your bottom line is—let’s get to it—your school can reject a child because their parents are homosexual.”
Reaves responded, “The bottom line is, if it’s a public benefit” balanced against the “sincere religious belief” of the church, then the church’s beliefs should prevail.
Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who wrote the three decisions expanding private school choice programs to include religious schools, and who dissented when the court recognized same-sex marriage, asked tough questions of both sides.
But the court’s five other conservatives—Justices Clarence Thomas, Neil M. Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett in addition to Alito and Kavanaugh—suggested their support for the challengers.
A decision in the case is expected by next June.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Backs Catholic Preschools in Colorado Funding Case
sources.text:
The Supreme Court offered clear support for Catholic preschools shut out of Colorado's preschool funding over faith-based admissions, a religious liberty fight with national stakes.
During a two-hour hearing in Washington, the Court's conservative majority pressed Colorado over a state preschool program that effectively bars Catholic schools unless they abandon core teachings on marriage and family. Fox News reported that the justices appeared ready to side with the religious plaintiffs in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.
The dispute centers on Colorado's Universal Preschool Program, created by a 2020 ballot measure. The program pays about $6,300 a year per child for up to 15 hours a week of preschool, funded by a tobacco tax. Schools that take the money must give every eligible child an equal chance to enroll, without regard to sexual orientation or gender identity.
Catholic parishes and the Archdiocese of Denver say that rule forces them to choose between public aid and their faith. Their schools admit only families who support Catholic teaching on same-sex relationships and gender. They call the exclusion religious discrimination under the First Amendment. The Supreme Court has weighed other high-stakes federal power fights in recent terms, and this case fits that pattern of constitutional scrutiny.
Colorado answers that the conditions are neutral and apply to every publicly funded preschool, religious or secular. State lawyer Helen Norton told the Court the state welcomes religious schools.
"Colorado welcomes religious preschools. The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike."
The state's position did not land cleanly with several justices.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh questioned why Colorado would manufacture a conflict when parents already have choices. He pointed to roughly 2,000 schools in the state and asked why the government needed to corner religious believers.
"Why not seek the win/win? There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 schools an appropriate fit for their children."
Kavanaugh called the state's approach a solution in search of a problem. He said families can find a good school that fits them while religious rights are still respected. No one has to lose for someone else to win.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett zeroed in on the practical effect. She asked the state to explain the difference between openly banning Catholic schools and writing conditions those schools cannot accept. Just the News noted that Barrett and Chief Justice John Roberts both treated the two approaches as nearly the same under free-exercise protections.
"Explain what the difference is between [explicitly excluding Catholic schools] and then choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools will be unable to agree to?"
Roberts has asked hard questions of both sides. He noted that earlier cases involved laws that openly singled out religious schools. Colorado's rule does not do that on its face. Still, he also observed that the real-world result can look a lot like the exclusion the Court has already rejected.
The Trump administration has signaled support for the religious plaintiffs. The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty is representing them. That backing lands as the Court continues to police the line between state power and constitutional rights, including in matters such as the administration's emergency filings on election procedures.
Erika Nagle, a parent at a Littleton Catholic preschool, told reporters her family lives the cost of the policy. Two of her children were denied access to the state funding. The family covers the extra expense. She said two archdiocese preschools have already closed.
"We are being excluded from this benefit because we are Catholic. And so in a state that preaches inclusion, they are actively going out of their way to exclude a huge chunk of people because of our religious beliefs."
Nagle described the funding as a carrot dangled in front of parents, one that pushes families to leave the Catholic education they want. Becket has argued that enrollment at archdiocesan preschools has fallen 20 percent and that two schools have shuttered. The archdiocese manages 34 preschools.
Colorado counters that many religious providers still take part. Officials point to Catholic Charities, at least three dozen Christian schools, one Muslim school, and three Jewish schools in the program. The state says religious schools remain free to join if they follow the same nondiscrimination rules that cover low-income and disabled students.
Plaintiffs and their allies call that framing incomplete. They note the program allows other enrollment priorities, for disabilities, low-income families, and other groups, while treating Catholic teaching on marriage as disqualifying. Breitbart reported that the schools and the Archdiocese of Denver tie their admissions rules to religious teaching on same-sex marriage and say the exclusion violates free-exercise rights.
The case asks the Court whether to narrow a 36-year-old precedent holding that religious practices do not create exemptions from broadly applicable laws. Lower courts rejected the Free Exercise challenge under that framework. Plaintiffs say the result guts later rulings that bar governments from shutting religious schools out of benefit programs because of how they exercise their faith.
National Review argued that Colorado's design is religious discrimination dressed up as neutrality, and that the program grants secular priorities while denying parallel space for Catholic conviction. Carrie Campbell Severino wrote that Carson held governments cannot exclude religious schools from benefit programs because of their religious exercise.
Liberal justices struck a different note. Justice Sonia Sotomayor pressed the plaintiffs' lawyer on Catholic teaching and parental choice. She said she struggled to see why a homosexual family would pick one of these schools, but insisted that should be the family's choice, not the school's power to exclude while taking public money.
"I'm hard-pressed to think that, given those [Catholic] teachings, that any homosexual family is going to choose to go to one of these schools, but that should be their choice, not your choice to exclude them."
Sotomayor framed the request as seeking an official state statement that public money will subsidize a right to reject children. Justice Elena Kagan drew a related line. She said the Court already knows you cannot treat religious institutions worse. The live question, in her view, is whether the state must treat them better.
Chief Justice Roberts reminded counsel that prior cases featured laws that expressly discriminated against religious schools on their face. "That's not the case here," he said. His vote could prove decisive. The Court's recent orders on election rules have shown how closely divided benches can still deliver clear results when the constitutional stakes are plain.
This is not Colorado's first trip to the Supreme Court over anti-discrimination rules and religious objectors. The Court has already backed a Colorado baker, a mental health counselor, and a website developer who challenged the state's policies. The Washington Examiner reported that a loss here could mark the state's fourth major First Amendment defeat at the high court in a decade.
The pattern matters. When a state repeatedly writes "neutral" rules that only traditional religious institutions cannot meet, the free-exercise problem stops looking accidental. Catholic schools are not asking for a special veto over other parents' lives. They are asking to keep their own character while the state runs a generally available benefit.
Kavanaugh's "win/win" point cuts to the incentive structure. Colorado has a large market of preschool options. LGBT parents can choose schools that match their values. Catholic parents can do the same. The state creates the collision by tying public money to a condition it knows sincere Catholic schools cannot accept, then calling the refusal bigotry.
The First Amendment text still anchors the claim: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof. The same principle binds the states. A funding program that is open in theory but closed in practice to churches that teach historic Christian doctrine on marriage is not a minor paperwork dispute. It is a test of whether free exercise still has force when the politics run the other way.
A ruling is expected by next spring. The Court will decide how far a state may go in attaching cultural conditions to a public benefit, and whether a decades-old precedent still blocks relief when the burden falls on religious schools alone. Related institutional fights continue on other fronts, including when the Court declined to revive a Biden-era deportation pause, but the preschool case turns on a cleaner free-exercise question.
Parents who want a Catholic education should not have to underwrite a state lecture on belief. If Colorado can fund preschool broadly, it can do so without kneecapping the schools that refuse to rewrite their faith.

sources.news_title: SCOTUS prepared to rule publicly funded religious schools can reject children of same-sex couples
sources.text:
Supreme Court prepared to rule that publicly funded religious schools can reject children of same-sex couples
A majority of the Supreme Court signaled on Tuesday that it would allow Catholic preschools receiving taxpayer money to deny enrollment to children of same-sex couples, potentially delivering another significant win for religious rights in schools.
The court’s conservative majority was unconvinced that a Colorado law, which bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender in publicly funded preschools, could be squared with recent high-profile precedents that expanded the ability of those religious schools to receive public money.
Broadly, the case represents a clash between First Amendment religious protections and laws intended to protect gay and transgender Americans from discrimination. When those conflicts have come to the Supreme Court in recent years, religious claims have won time after time. And there was no indication over the course of two hours of an Election Day oral argument that the Colorado dispute would be any different.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, at one point, questioned why Colorado had “provoked” the confrontation and missed a “win-win” by enforcing the discrimination provision and not allowing Catholic schools to opt out to “respect religious rights.”
“It seems like this is a would-be solution in search of a problem,” Kavanaugh, a member of the court’s conservative wing, told the Colorado attorney defending the state law. “I’m just trying to figure out why we’re here.”
In many ways, though, the case was of the court’s own making. For years, the conservative majority has expanded the ability of religious schools to receive public funding — chipping away at a wall many Americans understood to have long separated church and state. But those decisions largely steered clear of questions about what would happen when those publicly funded religious schools declined to enroll the child of a gay couple or use a student’s preferred pronoun in the classroom.
Sensing that Colorado’s argument was likely a lost cause, the court’s three-justice liberal wing repeatedly leaned into an attorney representing the Catholic parish and a Colorado family that sued to challenge the state’s anti-discrimination law.
“What you’re basically saying is, ‘We can exclude people merely because the exposure to them would cause us harm’ — that’s really what you’re saying,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor told the attorney for the Trump administration, which opposes Colorado’s law. “That is completely what you’re saying: We can exclude children of same-sex marriage, we can exclude children who might have transgender feelings or beliefs because exposing other children to them creates a problem.”
Sarah Harris, arguing for the Justice Department, rejected that framing. Instead, she said, the Catholic schools were exercising their religion by “requiring parents to agree with a school that they’re going to adhere to tenets of the Catholic faith and act consistently with them.”
Colorado enacted a ballot provision in 2020 that provides state funding for a universal preschool program, allowing both public and private schools to take part. The program includes a nondiscrimination provision that requires each school receiving public money to provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll, regardless of race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity and other factors.
The appeal, filed by the religious public interest firm Becket, appeared ready-made for a 6-3 conservative court that has repeatedly sided with religious interests. In one series of decisions, the court has made clear that when the government opens educational funding programs up to public and private schools, it cannot bar religious schools from taking part just because they are religious or offer religious instruction. The court in 2022, for instance, barred Maine from excluding religious schools from a tuition assistance program that allows parents to use vouchers to send their children to public or private schools.
Maine responded to that decision by embracing language like Colorado’s, technically allowing religious schools to take part but imposing anti-discrimination language the Catholic Church says it cannot bear.
Colorado’s history of cases involving religion and LGBTQ issues
At least some conservative justices seemed frustrated with the idea that states could be using such anti-discrimination provisions as a pretext to bar religious participation.
“If you know that the effect of choosing that requirement will push out those with contrary beliefs, how is that different?” conservative Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Colorado’s deputy solicitor general, Helen Norton.
Norton said there is “zero evidence” that the state targeted religious schools with its anti-discrimination language. She noted the state encouraged religious schools to take part, and that some religious schools — including Catholic schools — were engaged in the program. And Colorado’s anti-discrimination provision, she said, was enacted before the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in the Maine case.
A decision in the Colorado dispute is expected by the end of June.
A few conservative justices noted that many claims pitting religious rights against LGBTQ Americans had come from Colorado in recent years. Justice Samuel Alito, among the court’s most ardent defenders of religious rights, pressed Norton about her “state’s record in recent First Amendment cases,” ticking through a list that included an opinion this year endorsing a religious counselor’s challenge to Colorado’s ban on “conversion therapy” and a 2018 decision in which the court ruled in favor of a Colorado baker who refused to bake a cake to celebrate the marriage of a same-sex couple.
“What should we make of all of this?” Alito asked.
“Your honor,” Norton said, “there is no evidence of any sort of any religious hostility or animus” in the state’s preschool program.
Justice Elena Kagan, a member of the court’s liberal wing, seemed concerned about the long-term consequences of a loss for Colorado. She speculated that the next case could involve a family whose child was enrolled in a public school and who argued that allowing their child to attend classes alongside a gay or transgender peer burdened their religion.
“It’s going to be pretty easy for religious groups or religious individuals to come forward and say this would be a substantial burden on my religious beliefs,” Kagan said. “With respect to public schools alone, these inquiries could go on forever.”

sources.news_title: Court seems poised to side with Catholic preschools in religious discrimination dispute
sources.text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared ready to hold that the exclusion of Catholic preschools in Colorado from the state’s universal preschool program violates the First Amendment. After just over two hours of oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a majority seemed to agree with the challengers that Colorado’s refusal to provide them with an exemption from rules that would require the preschools to admit all students – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents – should be subject to a more stringent constitutional test than that applied by the lower court. The court could decide to apply that standard itself or send the case back to the lower courts for them to do so.
Colorado launched the universal preschool program, which provides families in the state with up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools, in 2023. To participate in the program, preschools must meet a variety of state standards and sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” The preschools cannot decline to serve LGBTQ families, because Colorado believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.
The plaintiffs – the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children – went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy. They contended that requiring Catholic preschools to agree to the nondiscrimination agreement to participate in the universal preschool program constitutes unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to carve out a religious exemption that allows them to take part in the program.
After both the district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the challengers’ claim, they came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to take up the case – which the court agreed in April 2026 to do.
Representing the challengers, Nicholas Reaves told the justices that the schools in the Archdiocese of Denver “exist to pass on the faith to the next generation.” “[T]his is not a zero-sum game,” he said, because “letting Catholic schools” participate in the universal preschool program “will create more seats for everyone.”
Representing the state, Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton countered that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools to” the program and allows them to teach their religious beliefs. It simply asks them, she emphasized, to comply with the same rules as everyone else.
One of the major points of contention at Tuesday’s argument was the significance of the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction. The case was the third in a trilogy of decisions on the availability of public funding for religious institutions. In Carson, the majority applied strict scrutiny – the toughest constitutional test – after it concluded that the Maine law barred some private schools from receiving public funds “solely because they are religious.”
In response to a question from Justice Clarence Thomas about whether a ruling for the challengers would require the court to extend its ruling in Carson, Reaves responded that it would not. In Carson, he insisted, the court’s “focus … was to look at … what is happening to the religious believer?” The court in Carson, he said, “didn’t focus on the text of the law in Maine. It focused on whether schools are being excluded on account of their religious exercise.”
Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Reaves on that point, observing that the law at issue in Carson specifically discriminated against religious schools – which, Roberts suggested, is not the case with the Colorado program.
Reaves pushed back. He noted that the laws in other cases involving public benefits had been neutral, rather than discriminating against religious people or organizations – for example, the court’s 1963 decision in Sherbert v. Verner, reversing a ruling by the South Carolina Supreme Court that had rejected a constitutional challenge to the denial of employment benefits from a Seventh-day Adventist whose religion barred her from working on Saturday.
Roberts later questioned Norton on a related point, asking her to differentiate the Colorado program from the law at issue in Carson and telling her that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here.” He also told Norton that the state was trying to “bury Sherbert” even though “nothing in our precedent has backed away from” it.
Two of the court’s Democratic appointees, however, echoed Roberts’ initial skepticism that Carson dictated the outcome of the challengers’ case. Justice Elena Kagan told Reaves that the trilogy of cases culminating in Carson involved laws that had excluded religious institutions and schools because of their religion. “[I]t was a nondiscrimination principle,” she emphasized, but “you’re asking us to” issue a decision that would go “far beyond” its earlier cases. In particular, she suggested, the challengers were seeking a ruling that religious people “need a special accommodation” because of their faith.
Reaves responded that an interpretation of the court’s decision in Carson that focused on whether the law at issue expressly discriminated against religion would be “very easy to circumvent.”
Kagan responded that this isn’t “a good case to raise the kind of specter of circumvention.” “[T]his is a case,” she continued, “of a state trying to enforce its own nondiscrimination principles.”
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to agree. She characterized Carson as a case that prohibited governments from treating religious schools worse than it treated secular schools. That doctrine, she posited, was “pretty narrow” and made “perfect sense.” But, she told Reaves, “your schools want to discriminate by exclusion” when no other school participating in the universal preschool program does so.
Some of the court’s Republican appointees were more persuaded by the challengers’ argument – also advanced by Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the challengers – that Carson should apply even if the Colorado law does not specifically target religion.
Justice Neil Gorsuch, for example, asked “what would be left” of cases like Sherbert “if everything turned on express discrimination” against religion, while Justice Samuel Alito appeared dubious that the legislators who enacted the Colorado universal preschool law “would not understand what the effect of” the law’s requirements “would be.”
Similarly, Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Norton why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows “schools will be unable to agree to?” Barrett pointed to a New York Times op-ed written in the wake of Carson by law professor Aaron Tang, who she stated suggested that states counteract some of the effects of Carson by enacting nondiscrimination requirements.
Norton resisted any effort to link Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement to an intent to target religious schools, stressing that there was no evidence of the legislature’s motives and (in response to a question from Jackson) that the requirement predated the inclusion of religious schools in the program.
The justices and advocates also debated, although less extensively than the significance of Carson, whether Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that are subject to a less stringent constitutional test, known as rational-basis review.
Reaves told the justices that the Colorado nondiscrimination requirement was not the kind of “across-the-board” prohibition that the court envisioned in Smith because the Colorado law contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catch-all” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation. Moreover, he added, the law also creates exceptions to accommodate children with disabilities and children from low-income families.
For her part, Norton characterized the preferences as very different from the kind of exclusion that the challengers seek. Even if a school receives a preference, she stressed, it is still subject to the nondiscrimination requirement.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh appeared to approach the case from what he regarded as a practical angle, asking Norton why the state wouldn’t “seek the win/win?” With over 2,000 preschools participating in the Colorado program, he said, there should be “plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers” and, at the same time, “the ability of LGBT parents” to find a school that is a good fit for their families. “Why,” he asked, “has this been provoked?”
Justice Sonia Sotomayor took a different tack, suggesting that a ruling for the challengers could have broader implications. A Catholic preschool, she told Reaves, could reject a child “merely” because his or her parents are LGBTQ. Would this, she queried, also allow a religious preschool to turn down Black children?
Reaves said that it would not. He pointed to a 1983 case in which the Supreme Court, applying strict scrutiny, upheld the Internal Revenue Service’s decision to revoke the tax-exempt status of a private university and private school with racially discriminatory admissions policies. The government in that case, he emphasized, indicated that its interest in prohibiting such policies was not merely “compelling” (the first factor under strict scrutiny) but “overriding.”
He told the justices that strict scrutiny should similarly apply to this case. “And then the government can come forward and say we have a really good reason for” excluding Catholic preschools from the program. But, he concluded, “we just don’t think they’ve done that in this case.”
By the end of the argument, Sotomayor seemed to leave little doubt about where she stood. “No matter what line of cases we follow,” she said, “there will be tremendous problems and a great cost to someone.”
A decision is expected sometime next year.

The Supreme Court's conservative majority offered clear support Tuesday for Catholic preschools that claim Colorado's taxpayer-funded program improperly excludes them by unconstitutionally intruding on their religious rights.
At issue is whether those private education institutions that deny admission to children of LGBTQ+ parents violate state anti-discrimination laws, and can therefore be denied a generally applicable public benefit.
It is the latest high-profile religious rights appeal to reach the high court in recent years, several of them originating from Colorado.
2026 MIDTERM ELECTION DAY RESULTS: LIVE UPDATES
In a lively two-hour oral argument, the justices debated competing interests involving both religious liberty and a state's interest in ensuring equal opportunity for gay and lesbian parents.
"I'm hard-pressed to think that, given those [Catholic] teachings, that any homosexual family is going to choose to go to one of these schools, but that should be their choice, not your choice to exclude them," said Justice Sonia Sotomayor to the lawyer for the plaintiffs. "That's what you're asking for... You want an official statement by the State that I will subsidize you with public money even though – because I have a right to reject children."
ANDREA PICCIOTTI-BAYER: COLORADO'S UNIVERSAL PRESCHOOL REVIVES VILE ANTI-CATHOLIC LAWS
But Justice Brett Kavanaugh said the state's motives, however well-intentioned, are promoting a kind of conformity that is not constitutionally permissible.
"Why not seek the win/win?" Kavanaugh asked the attorney for the state. "There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 [Colorado] schools an appropriate fit for their children.
"It seems like this is a would-be solution in search of a problem that is unnecessary to create this clash," he added. "There's an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school that's a fit for them, and respect religious rights."
CATHOLIC SCHOOLS, BANNED RIFLES AND ‘CLIMATE LAWFARE’: BLOCKBUSTER FIGHTS AWAIT SUPREME COURT
Colorado established a Universal Preschool Program (UPK) in a 2020 ballot measure, distributing public funds for participating schools, with the requirement they "provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability."
Two Catholic parishes sued, arguing the policy targets their sincerely held beliefs about same-sex marriage.
The archdiocese in the state manages 34 preschools, with a policy to only admit students from families who support Catholic ideology, including on same-sex relationships and gender identity.
They seek exemptions to the Colorado law, arguing their exclusion is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment.
The Trump administration has signaled its support of the religious plaintiffs.
The state counters its public benefit conditions are neutral and generally applied to every preschool.
It provides a $6,300 annual benefit per child for up to 15 hours a week of preschool, with money coming from a tobacco tax.
Officials told the nine-member bench that religious schools are free to participate but must abide by nondiscrimination laws, similar to those affecting low-income and disabled students.
As part of its review of the Colorado dispute, the high court will decide whether to narrow a 36-year-old precedent that religious practices do not create exemptions from broadly applicable laws.
The First Amendment states, "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof."
The Supreme Court in prior decades had focused on the first part, ensuring a constitutional separation of church and state, when disputes over religious rights reached the public sphere.
But the current conservative bench in the past few years — led by Justice Samuel Alito — has trended toward favoring religious institutions raising "free exercise" claims.
The justices have separately backed a Colorado baker, mental health counselor and website developer, who all challenged the state's anti-discrimination policies.
The oral arguments Tuesday seemed to divide along ideological lines.
Conservative justices focused on the "free exercise" claims by the Catholic parishes that state requirements for receiving public benefits amounted to religious discrimination.
"Explain what the difference is between [explicitly excluding Catholic schools] and then choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools will be unable to agree to?" said Justice Amy Coney Barrett.
But Justice Elena Kagan cited the court's prior cases, which she said affirmed the idea "you can't treat religious institutions differently."
"That's not the principle that's at issue here," Kagan said. "The principle at issue here is: Do you have to treat them better?"
Chief Justice John Roberts asked tough questions of both sides and his vote could prove determinative. At one point, he expressed skepticism that recent rulings favoring the rights of religious schools over similar claims should also prevail in the current petition.
"The law in those cases, in each of them, expressly discriminated against religious schools on its face," Roberts told Reaves. "That's not the case here," suggesting Colorado's law may be applied fairly across the board.
The current dispute was brought by plaintiffs including St. Mary Catholic School.
Erika Nagle, whose children attend the Littleton facility, told Fox News Digital that two of her children were denied access to the state's preschool funding program, leaving her family to cover additional education expenses.
"We are being excluded from this benefit because we are Catholic," Nagle said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "And so in a state that preaches inclusion, they are actively going out of their way to exclude a huge chunk of people because of our religious beliefs.
"We have had two preschools in the archdiocese that have been closed down," she added. "The state is dangling a carrot over here, incentivizing people to leave their faith, to abandon the Catholic education that they want."
The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty represented the plaintiffs in court, arguing the state's policies are having severe consequences, with enrollment at archdiocesan preschools falling 20% and two schools shuttered.

The state counters that religious entities like Catholic Charities, at least three dozen Christian schools, one Muslim and three Jewish schools continue to participate in the preschool funding program.
"Colorado welcomes religious preschools" to its program, state attorney Helen Norton told the high court. "The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike."

sources.news_title: Supreme Court hears clash between Catholic preschools, Colorado over ‘universal’ program
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (OSV News) — The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments Nov. 3 in a case over a clash between Catholic preschools and the state of Colorado over whether those schools can participate in the state’s universal preschool program.
The program provides funds — up to about $6,000 — to parents to send their child to the preschool of their choice, public or private, including faith-based schools.
Two Catholic parishes with preschools in the Archdiocese of Denver have alleged the state of Colorado excluded the religious preschools from participating in the program due to their religious beliefs. The schools require faculty and parents to sign a “statement of community beliefs” acknowledging the Catholic Church’s teachings on topics including marriage, sexuality and gender.
But Colorado has argued the Catholic preschools ran afoul of a nondiscrimination rule in the program that prohibits participating schools from refusing admission to any child on the basis of the sexual orientation and gender identity of the child or the child’s family.
“The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation,” Nicholas Reaves, senior counsel at Becket, a religious liberty law firm representing the schools, said during oral arguments. “To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the Church’s teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the state has denied Colorado families the ability to use universal preschool funding at Catholic schools.”
Basis of opposition to Colorado policy questioned
Justice Sonia Sotomayor pressed Reaves, arguing, “The Catholic schools are not being excluded on their face. They’re choosing not to participate, because they won’t get an exemption.”
“For the Catholic Church, it’s not about excluding anyone based on who they are,” he replied.
Sotomayor continued, “They’re saying we’ll exclude your children, if their parents are homosexual.”
Reaves said, “All families, regardless of who they are, even if they’re Catholic, have to agree to the statement of community beliefs in good faith. That’s the requirement.”
According to the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith’s 2024 declaration, “Dignitas Infinita” (“Infinite Dignity”), the Catholic Church holds “that every person, regardless of sexual orientation, ought to be respected in his or her dignity and treated with consideration, while ‘every sign of unjust discrimination’ is to be carefully avoided,” but opposes what it calls “gender theory.” The teaching document described sexual difference as “the greatest possible difference that exists between living beings,” which in humans “becomes the source of that miracle that never ceases to surprise us: the arrival of new human beings in the world.”
Justices question lawfulness of Colorado policy
Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton argued that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools” to the program, sometimes called UPK.
“The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike. UPK is neutral towards religion,” Norton said.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh questioned Norton on whether Colorado’s position was consistent with allowing single-sex preschools to participate in the program. Norton replied that biological sex is “not one of the characteristics enumerated in the UPK law.”
But more justices appeared inclined toward the preschools’ position. Chief Justice John Roberts remarked the effect of Colorado’s law seemed “pretty much the same” as a Maine law the court struck down in its 2022 Carson v. Makin decision. The court found that law improperly excluded religious schools from a public tuition assistance program.
Supreme Court to decide by next June
Kelley Robinson, president of the Human Rights Campaign, an LGBTQ+ advocacy group, argued in a Nov. 3 statement that the case “is straightforward — schools receiving public funds from a state universal preschool program cannot be allowed to use taxpayer dollars to leave LGBTQ+ families behind.”
“As the arguments made clear today, Colorado’s non-discrimination requirement ensures no family can be denied a quality education simply for who they are — it is lawful and should be upheld. Exclusion has no place in our educational system,” Robinson said.
During a brief press conference after oral arguments, Reaves likened Colorado’s position to a “‘no Catholics need apply’ policy.”
Colorado, he said, “argued that Catholic schools must abandon their religious exercise to participate in a program open to everyone else. It claimed that Catholic schools are the ones excluding families, even as Colorado excludes thousands of Catholic families, and it insisted with a straight face that a program can still be universal while shutting out families for their faith.”
Oral arguments took place the same day as the Nov. 3 elections.
A decision in the case is expected by the end of the Supreme Court’s term, which typically ends in June.
Kate Scanlon is a national reporter for OSV News covering Washington. Follow her on X @kgscanlon.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court weighs if Colorado program can force Christian preschools to adopt LGBT nondiscrimination rules
Supreme Court weighs religious exemptions to LGBTQ nondiscrimination protections in Colo. preschool case
sources.text:
U.S. Supreme Court
Supreme Court weighs religious exemptions to LGBTQ nondiscrimination protections in Colo. preschool case
Ruling expected by June 2027
The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments Tuesday in a case examining whether Colorado’s exclusion of religious preschools from a publicly funded education program violates the First Amendment’s guarantee of religious freedom.
In St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, Catholic preschools in Colorado have brought the fight to the nation’s highest court, arguing that their exclusion from the state’s universal preschool program, including its public funding, amounts to religious discrimination that violates their First Amendment rights.
The Catholic schools want to participate in the program and receive public funding while maintaining admissions policies that require families to support Catholic teachings on marriage, sexuality, and gender. Those policies conflict with the program’s equal-opportunity requirements, which prohibit discrimination based on characteristics including sexual orientation and gender identity.
Under the program, Colorado provides 15 hours of preschool per week for eligible children through participating public and private providers. The program allows families to select their preferred preschool, provided the school meets certain requirements, including equal-opportunity standards. The benefit has been valued at approximately $6,000 per child annually, according to attorneys representing the Catholic schools.
The plaintiffs in the case include St. Mary Catholic Parish, St. Bernadette Catholic Parish, the Archdiocese of Denver, and two parents of preschool-aged children. They went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy, arguing that making the Catholic preschools’ participation in the universal preschool program contingent on accepting the equal-opportunity requirements amounts to unlawful religious discrimination.
They argue that the First Amendment requires Colorado to provide a religious exemption to the nondiscrimination requirements so the schools can participate in the program without compromising their religious beliefs.
The schools also argue that Colorado permits certain enrollment preferences for secular purposes while refusing to accommodate their religious admissions policies.
The 10th U.S. Court of Appeals ruled in favor of Colorado in September 2025, upholding the state’s equal-opportunity requirements.
The 10th Circuit acknowledged that the Supreme Court has consistently held that states cannot categorically exclude religious institutions from otherwise available public benefits because of their religious character. However, it determined that Colorado was not explicitly excluding the schools because they were religious institutions. Rather, the schools were ineligible because their admissions policies did not comply with the program’s nondiscrimination requirements.
In the state’s view, these schools can participate in the preschool program provided they abide by the same equal-opportunity requirements imposed on other participating providers. Colorado argued that its restrictions apply to enrollment policies and conduct across the program and are not specifically targeted at religious institutions or religious practices.
The case requires the Supreme Court to consider several previous decisions involving religious freedom and the government’s ability to enforce generally applicable laws.
In 1990, the Supreme Court held in Employment Division v. Smith that neutral, generally applicable laws do not violate the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause simply because they place a burden on someone’s religious practices.
The case involved two men who worked at a private drug rehabilitation organization and were fired after ingesting peyote, a hallucinogenic substance, during a religious ceremony of the Native American Church. Oregon subsequently denied them unemployment benefits because their drug use constituted work-related misconduct. The Supreme Court ruled that the state’s denial did not violate their First Amendment rights.
Another ruling relevant to this case is the Supreme Court’s 2020 decision in Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue. The court ruled that Montana could not exclude religious schools from a generally available scholarship program solely because of their religious status. The decision held that doing so violated the Constitution’s Free Exercise Clause.
Another significant precedent is Carson v. Makin, in which the Supreme Court ruled in 2022 that Maine could not exclude religious schools from its public tuition-assistance program simply because they provided religious instruction. The state’s requirement that participating private schools be “nonsectarian” violated the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause.
The 6-3 decision was opposed by three justices, who argued that the ruling would require taxpayers to fund religious education and undermine the separation between church and state.
The Supreme Court’s decision in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy could further clarify how these precedents apply when states condition public funding on compliance with nondiscrimination requirements.
The court agreed to consider two specific questions: whether Colorado’s treatment of certain secular enrollment preferences undermines the general applicability of its nondiscrimination requirements under Employment Division v. Smith, and whether Carson v. Makin applies when the government does not explicitly exclude religious institutions from public benefits.
The ruling could have implications beyond Colorado’s preschool program, particularly for the ability of state and federal governments to enforce nondiscrimination requirements against religious organizations receiving public funding.
The Supreme Court is expected to issue a decision by the end of June 2027.
LGBTQ advocates weigh potential consequences
The Washington Blade spoke with Meg York, chief legal and policy officer of COLAGE, a national nonprofit organization that unites and supports people with LGBTQ parents. COLAGE filed an amicus brief in the case. York attended Tuesday’s oral arguments and discussed what she heard from the justices and the potential implications for LGBTQ families.
York emphasized that Colorado’s decision to include Catholic schools in its universal preschool program is an important distinction in the case, arguing that the dispute should not be characterized as a simple conflict between religious institutions and the state.
“Colorado explicitly chose to include Catholic schools in its universal pre-K program, so when we talk about the Catholic arguments, I think there’s maybe a false binary there that it’s one versus the other,” she told the Blade during a phone interview. “But in terms of the arguments raised by the petitioners or the respondents, I was listening to see if there was anybody who seemed to be kind of straying from what we typically expect in ideological lines, and I’m not sure that I heard that in this case.”
When asked how she interpreted the justices’ questions and what they could indicate about the eventual outcome, York said she saw some potential for the court to take a narrower approach that considers Colorado’s arguments.
“I do think that there were times at which I felt that some of the justices were potentially more receptive to really taking a more narrow approach to this case and really thinking about the arguments that Colorado was putting forward. I think there were some moments of hope. It’s hard when you’re in an oral argument. You hear some questions, but then there’s a lot of silence, too. It can be difficult to know which way certain folks are leaning or not.”
One of the central legal disputes involves whether Colorado’s equal-opportunity requirements are generally applicable or whether the state makes exceptions that could require it to accommodate religious admissions policies.
York disputed the characterization of the state’s provisions as exemptions, saying Colorado views them as measures intended to advance equal access rather than exceptions to its nondiscrimination requirements.
“I don’t think the state of Colorado was classifying them or framing them as exemptions as much as they were the kind of things that could advance their equal opportunity goals. So, you know, there were no exemptions to the nondiscrimination requirement, none at all. Colorado doesn’t give any exemptions to that. And so when they talk about schools that help serve low-income individuals or individuals with disabilities, those are all in furtherance of the equal opportunities that Colorado seeks to advance.”
The arguments also raised questions about how a ruling could affect nondiscrimination protections beyond the preschool program. Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor raised concerns about how religious exemptions could affect laws designed to protect people based on characteristics such as sexual orientation and gender identity.
York pointed to those exchanges as particularly significant, questioning whether a broader interpretation of religious exemptions could subject more nondiscrimination laws to heightened constitutional scrutiny.
“Some of the concerns raised by Justice Jackson and also by Justice Sotomayor were about this idea of when you have protections or when you have a nondiscrimination law to protect people who have protected characteristics, that we’re not really in the business of determining whose belief is a sincerely held religious belief. So does that push everything to strict scrutiny? And I think there were some concerns about that.”
The case also puts two major lines of Supreme Court precedent under scrutiny: Employment Division v. Smith, the 1990 decision involving neutral, generally applicable laws, and Carson v. Makin, the 2022 decision prohibiting states from excluding religious schools from public benefits because of their religious instruction.
York noted that the justices grappled with how those decisions apply to Colorado’s program. She also emphasized that the Supreme Court declined to consider the plaintiffs’ separate request to overturn Employment Division v. Smith.
“In some ways, you have the petitioners who were kind of saying that the Carson line of cases is controlling, but then they were a little mushy in some of the cases being cited in that line of cases. We certainly heard the court grappling with what they consider when they’re considering Employment Division v. Smith. Does Carson make a reply here when you have very different circumstances under which that opinion was issued?”
For York, the case ultimately presents questions about how religious freedom and equal access can coexist, particularly when public funding is involved.
She said COLAGE believes LGBTQ families should be protected under nondiscrimination laws without requiring religious institutions to sacrifice their constitutional protections.
“My organization takes the position that religious freedom is something that we all value. Whether you are a specific religion or whether you are not religious, that is part of the freedoms that are guaranteed to us in the Constitution, and that’s something that benefits all of us. To that end, we feel that people with LGBTQ parents should be protected under the law, and that is exactly the heart of these nondiscrimination laws. And at the same time, that doesn’t mean that we need to sacrifice religious liberty or religious freedom to do so.”
York said she believes the case’s ultimate impact will depend heavily on how narrowly or broadly the justices write their decision.
“I don’t think it’s a foregone conclusion that they’re going to rule in favor of St. Mary or in favor of the petitioners, but even if they did, we could get a very narrow ruling that is incredibly specific and limited.”
LGBTQ organizations warn of consequences for families
Other LGBTQ advocacy organizations also warned that allowing religious preschools to participate in publicly funded programs while maintaining admissions policies that conflict with nondiscrimination requirements could have consequences for families beyond Colorado.
The National Women’s Law Center argued that a ruling in favor of the Catholic schools could undermine equal access to publicly funded education and potentially create a precedent for excluding other families.
“No four-year-old child should be denied preschool placement because their parents are gay or lesbian,” said Brian Dittmeier, director of LGBTQI+ equality at NWLC. “Marriage equality is the law of the land, and the court should not open the door to extreme arguments that seek to chip away at equal rights for same-sex couples. All families deserve access to affordable, high-quality early care and education, which is exactly why Colorado voters mobilized to expand early education access in their state through this universal and incredibly successful program.”
Dittmeier also said Colorado’s faith-based preschools have previously complied with nondiscrimination requirements and warned that allowing exceptions could leave same-sex families with fewer options.
“For years, Colorado’s faith-based preschools have had no trouble complying with nondiscrimination requirements as a common condition of receiving taxpayer funding to support their operations. Allowing discrimination in a state program specifically intended to achieve universal access is counter to Colorado voters’ intent and will leave same-sex families with fewer options to support their children. The same reasoning could later be used to turn away other children, including children of unmarried mothers or children whose parents are divorced. Karen Loewy, senior counsel and director of constitutional law practice at Lambda Legal, said religious schools can maintain their own admissions criteria when privately funded but should be required to follow state nondiscrimination laws when accepting taxpayer money.

We pray the Supreme Court will end this discrimination and hold Colorado to its word.”

He argued that religious schools should not have to abandon their beliefs to receive those benefits.

We are confident that this discrimination won’t stand and that the court will hand Colorado yet another loss.”
