sources.news_title: US Supreme Court justices doubtful of Colorado rule in Catholic preschool case
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday in a Colorado case over the balance of protections for LGBTQ+ people and religion. (Photo by Jane Norman/States Newsroom)
Conservative U.S. Supreme Court justices appeared doubtful Tuesday of yet another Colorado policy involving the balance of state anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ+ people and religious exemptions.
The Archdiocese of Denver and two Catholic preschools say in a lawsuit that they were unable to participate in Colorado’s universal preschool program, known as UPK Colorado, because the state will not allow the religious educational institutions to exclude LGBTQ+ children and parents.
Attorneys for the schools and the state Tuesday argued before the Supreme Court about whether Colorado’s anti-discrimination policies improperly target Catholic schools for their sincerely held beliefs, violating the free exercise clause of the First Amendment, or if Colorado applied the requirement universally with no intention to exclude the schools.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh said that with 2,000 preschools and only 34 of them Catholic in Colorado, there are plentiful opportunities for families to find a preschool that suits their needs, so the state can respect both religious beliefs and the rights of LGBTQ+ parents.
“It seems like this is a … would-be solution in search of a problem that is unnecessary to create this clash,” Kavanaugh said. “Why has this been provoked when there’s an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school that’s a fit for them, and respect religious rights?”
Your Catholic schools will reject the child merely because their parents are homosexual.
– Justice Sonia Sotomayor
Nicholas Reaves, attorney with the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, who represents the plaintiffs in the case, said he does not think the state has presented a “really good reason” to prevent religious schools from receiving the public benefit of UPK funding, as is required by the legal standard of strict scrutiny. Sarah Harris, principal deputy solicitor general for the U.S. Justice Department, also argued before the court in support of the plaintiffs in the case.
Liberal justices said the Catholic schools are looking for a specific accommodation and exemption to a universally applied principle, while in previous cases, religious schools were just asking to be treated the same as other schools, Justice Elena Kagan said. Laws shut down by previous rulings explicitly discriminated against religious schools, while Colorado’s UPK rules do not.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said that many other religious schools, including Catholic schools, agreed to Colorado’s anti-discrimination provisions. Justice Sonia Sotomayor said the Catholic schools involved in the case chose not to participate in the program because they will not receive a special exemption allowing them to exclude children from a specific protected class.
“Your Catholic schools will reject the child merely because their parents are homosexual,” Sotomayor said. “If it’s a sincere religious exercise to exclude Blacks, this principle would permit the exclusion of those Black children.”
Religious preschools welcome
Helen Norton, deputy solicitor general for Colorado, argued that the state holds all preschools to the same standards, including teacher training, student-teacher ratios and equal opportunity. Religious schools are welcome to teach their beliefs on sex, gender and marriage. All of those standards are generally applicable to all participants.
“Colorado welcomes religious preschools to UPK,” Norton said. “The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike.”
The St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton and the St. Bernadette Catholic Parish in Lakewood both operate preschool programs that were not part of UPK since the state requires providers to accept applicants without regard to the family’s religion, sexual orientation or gender identity.
The schools applied for public funding through the universal preschool program and were denied when they requested religious exemptions from the state’s equal-opportunity rule. They claimed their rights under the free exercise clause of the First Amendment were violated by their exclusion.
A U.S. District Court of Colorado judge ruled in June 2024 that the UPK requirement that prohibits discrimination against LGBTQ+ families is valid. The Denver-based 10th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the district court’s decision in October 2025, and the Supreme Court accepted the case in April. The church and schools filed the lawsuit against Lisa Roy, executive director of the Colorado Department of Early Childhood.
The Supreme Court will weigh in on aspects of a 1990 ruling in another case that raised the question of religious exemptions to state laws. The court held in Employment Division v. Smith that a person’s religious beliefs are not an automatic exemption from compliance with a law against conduct the state is free to regulate. Attorneys for the state heavily relied on this ruling.
The initial lawsuit made several references to past cases related to LGBTQ+ discrimination in Colorado that made their way to the nation’s highest court. That includes a case in which the Supreme Court said a Colorado web designer does not have to make websites for same-sex couples, and another in which the court said a cake shop owner could deny a same-sex couple a wedding cake based on religious beliefs.
Most recently, the court sided with a Christian counselor against Colorado’s law that bans licensed providers from conducting “conversion therapy,” a discredited practice of trying to change a person’s sexual orientation, such as to eliminate same-sex attraction, or gender identity.
Conservative justices wondered how Colorado did not predict a conflict such as the one posed in the preschool case, given the state’s history of court challenges to LGBTQ+ protections.
Six of the justices on the Supreme Court are Catholic — five in the conservative majority, and one, Sotomayor, in the liberal minority. Justice Neil Gorsuch, who is Episcopalian, was raised Catholic.
The court is expected to announce a decision in the case by June.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court to rule on Catholic preschool protections – The...
sources.text:
The Supreme Court will hear arguments Tuesday in a case brought by Catholic preschools that say it’s unconstitutional to exclude them from a state-funded program over their admissions policy for LGBTQ+ families, the latest religious-rights case before the conservative-majority court.
Colorado says their refusal to admit kids from those families violates the state’s anti-discrimination law.
But St. Mary Catholic Parish and the Archdiocese of Denver argue that the policy is based on religious teachings about same-sex marriage and that excluding them violates their free-exercise rights.
President Donald Trump’s administration is supporting the Catholic institutions.
A win for the preschools could further narrow a landmark 1990 Supreme Court decision that found religious practices don’t create exemptions from laws that otherwise apply broadly. Written by conservative icon Justice Antonin Scalia in a case over the spiritual use of peyote, a cactus containing mescaline that’s sacred to many Indigenous people, the decision has nevertheless long been a target of the conservative legal movement.
In the Colorado case, the high court could be sympathetic to the schools. The justices have sided with religious schools in similar disputes before, ruling in recent years that they can’t be excluded from programs in Maine and Montana that provide public aid to private schools. In 2025, though, the court deadlocked over a plan to establish a publicly funded Catholic charter school after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself.
The Colorado universal preschool program was created by a 2020 ballot measure. It provides public funding for preschool at schools chosen by parents.
The plaintiffs, represented by the group Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, say the state has allowed other preschools to prioritize children with disabilities or those from low-income families, so admission based on religious beliefs about gender and same-sex marriage should be allowed, too. The Catholic preschools say their enrollment has dropped 20% since the program started.
Colorado argues that the other admissions decisions are in line with the state’s anti-discrimination rules.
The Associated Press contributed to this article

sources.news_title: Brett Kavanaugh asks Trump DOJ lawyer if religious exemptions offer "favor"
sources.text:
U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh pressed Department of Justice (DOJ) lawyer Sarah Harris about whether certain religious exemptions may constitute “favor” during arguments in the case St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy on Tuesday.
The case centers around the legal question of whether Colorado can exclude a Catholic preschool from a program granting public funding to preschools if it does not comply with nondiscrimination requirements regarding sexual orientation and gender identity.
The conservative-leaning court has sided with religious groups against LGBTQ+ rights in recent cases, including a ruling against Colorado in a legal dispute over a conversion therapy ban. The court's ruling on this case could have implications for LGBTQ+ nondiscrimination laws across the country.
Read More on News
Newsweek reached out to lawyers for the petitioners and respondents for comment via email.
What Is the Case About?
The case involves Catholic preschools and families arguing it is unconstitutional for Colorado to prohibit them from the taxpayer-funded free preschool program because of their admission policies on LGBTQ+ families and children. The program provides families with more than $6,000 to send their children to preschool.
The case was brought by Dan and Lisa Sheley, Catholic parents who have sent their children to school in St. Mary’s Catholic Parish and believe the program should provide their funds to attend that school. They wrote in a statement back in April, when the court agreed to hear the case, that the program has “cut out families like ours because we chose a Catholic education.”
Colorado has said it allows religious schools to participate in the program, but that they must follow nondiscrimination laws.
In their petition to the Supreme Court, petitioners argued the state law requires schools to ensure families have an “equal opportunity” to enroll but has granted numerous exceptions.
“But Colorado excludes Catholic preschools because they admit only families who support Catholic beliefs, including on sex and gender,” the petition reads.
Attorney General Phil Weiser’s office wrote in a filing the universal preschool program “affirmatively welcomes faith-based providers while allowing no exceptions from its equal-opportunity requirements.”
“Because this case involves neither any exceptions nor the discretion to create exceptions, it is not an appropriate vehicle for addressing the question of what sorts of exceptions would render the government’s action not generally applicable,” he wrote.
The Legal Questions Facing the Court
The court has been asked to address two questions in the case—whether “proving a lack of general applicability under Employment Division v. Smith requires showing unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct,” and whether Carson v. Makin “displaces the rule of Employment Division v. Smith only when the government explicitly excludes religious people and institutions.”
In Smith, the court ruled that governments can enforce laws even if they incidentally burden religious practices. In Carson v. Makin, the justices held that Maine cannot exclude religious schools from a tuition-assistance program because they are religious.
What Both Sides Argued
Nicholas Reaves, senior counsel at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, argued on behalf of the petitioners. He said Colorado families have been “denied” the ability to use the funding at Catholic schools because of “this sincere religious exercise.” He also pointed to examples of other schools being able to turn families away.
“Colorado's inconsistent and contradictory arguments further confirm the state's actions are anything but generally applicable. Colorado has flexibly interpreted the mandate to accommodate important secular interests, but it's called the same law a hard limit. When petitioners sought a religious accommodation,” he said.
Colorado has “refused to extend that flexible treatment to petitioners,” Reaves said.
Reaves wrote in a statement on Tuesday, “Colorado’s Catholics-need-not-apply rules make a mockery of our nation’s laws and commitment to religious freedom. The Supreme Court has been crystal clear: Americans don’t have to forfeit their faith to receive public benefits. We are confident that this discrimination won’t stand and that the Court will hand Colorado yet another loss.”
Meanwhile, Helen Norton, Colorado deputy solicitor general, said the state only asks that these schools comply with the same requirements that all publicly funded preschools must meet. The universal preschool program is “neutral” on religion.
“Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage, free to teach them while receiving public funding,” she said.
Norton said the program “does not devalue religion by allowing preschools to remove these barriers.”
What Did Brett Kavanaugh and Other Justices Say?
One of the central arguments the attorneys representing the petitioners faced is whether they believe religious schools have different treatment under the law. Kavanaugh referenced this during his questioning of Harris, the Justice Department’s principal deputy solicitor general.
“There's been some discussion, of is this a favor or is this treating them equally, or providing an accommodation, I guess another way to say it. So, if a Jewish service member is given Saturdays off, is that giving that service member a favor, or is that ensuring equal opportunity for that service member?” he asked.
Harris said that she views it as “ensuring vindication of free exercise rights and something that that person is compelled to do.”
“I don't think it's like a special favor to people to respect a First Amendment right. I disagree with the framing that there's some sort of impermissible thumb on the scale involved,” she said.
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson raised a similar question, telling Reaves she is “concerned” that these preschools are trying to do something the state determined violates its “principles with respect to discriminating against or excluding a certain group of people.”
“It seems to me you're asking for a special rule for religious schools that when Colorado says anyone who receives these funds has to be open to everyone and can't discriminate what you're asking for in the context of this free exercise claim, is a special rule for religious schools to be able to not follow that condition,” she said.
Reaves, however, said that is not what he is asking, pointing to previous cases in which the court has found that “if there is a sincere religious exercise that's being burdened, the government has to show a really good reason for doing that.”
How the Court Has Ruled on LGBTQ+ Cases
The court has weighed in on several legal matters involving LGBTQ+ rights in recent terms.
In March, liberal justices Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan joined the court’s conservative majority in a ruling in favor of a challenge of Colorado’s law prohibiting conversion therapy for minors.
The court held that the law, when applied to talk therapy provided by Kaley Chiles, who is a licensed counselor in Colorado, regulates speech based on viewpoint. The court said lower courts failed to apply "sufficiently rigorous" First Amendment scrutiny.
It also upheld Tennessee’s ban on gender‑affirming medical care for transgender minors in 2025.
Conservative Justice Clarence Thomas has signaled an openness to revisiting the case that legalized same-sex marriage nationwide, writing in the 2022 case Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization, "In future cases, we should reconsider all of this Court's substantive due process precedents, including Griswold, Lawrence, and Obergefell."
Conservative Justice Amy Coney Barrett has described marriage rights as “fundamental,” comments legal experts have interpreted to mean she is not inclined to overturn same-sex marriage.
Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Gabe Whisnant and Anthony Murray.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Justices Split Over Taxpayer Funding for Schools That Reject Children of LGBTQ+ Parents
sources.text:
This story originally appeared on The Advocate.
The U.S. Supreme Court’s three liberal justices sharply questioned Tuesday whether Catholic preschools should receive taxpayer funding while retaining the ability to reject children of LGBTQ+ parents. However, many of the conservatives appeared receptive to the schools’ challenge to Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirements.
The argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy exposed competing understandings of equality. It involved religious schools seeking public funding without compromising their beliefs, and families seeking the same educational opportunities as their neighbors.
“The principle at issue here is, do you have to treat them better?” Justice Elena Kagan asked.
Colorado launched its universal preschool program in 2023 through public and private providers, including religious schools. Participating schools may teach their faith but must provide equal enrollment opportunities regardless of protected characteristics, including sexual orientation and gender identity.
Two Catholic parishes and the Archdiocese of Denver challenged those conditions without applying to participate, arguing that they conflict with religious admissions policies. A federal district court ruled for Colorado after a trial, and the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed that decision. But the Supreme Court agreed in April to hear the challenge.
Earlier Supreme Court decisions barred states from excluding schools from funding because they are religious. Colorado argues that its program welcomes religious providers and regulates discriminatory admissions, not religious teaching.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor pressed the schools’ attorney, Nicholas Reaves, on what an exemption would permit.
Related: The Supreme Court is taking up a case that could shut LGBTQ+ families out of preschool
“Your Catholic schools will reject a child merely because their parents are homosexual?” she asked.
“I would say, if it’s the sincere religious exercise of the petitioner, then I think that would be permitted,” Reaves responded.
Reaves said families must affirm the schools’ statement of community beliefs in good faith. According to him, some circumstances involving same-sex couples would prevent enrollment.
Sotomayor distinguished instruction from exclusion.
“You can teach whatever it is you want to teach, but if parents choose to subject their children to this teaching, you have to accept that child,” she said. “That should be their choice, not your choice to exclude them.”
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson challenged the Trump administration’s argument that conditioning funding on compliance burdens religious freedom.
“The school itself does not have to admit anybody it doesn’t want to admit,” Jackson told Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who argued in support of the catholic schools. “But if they’re accepting public benefits voluntarily, these are the conditions that apply.”
Jackson asked whether the same reasoning could justify racial exclusions. Harris said racial discrimination would very likely produce a different outcome under strict scrutiny, the demanding constitutional test the administration wants applied.
“But that’s just arbitrary,” Jackson responded. “That’s just because the Court would say race is different, right?”
Kagan questioned the implications for public education.
“So is the next case parents in a public school saying it’s really important to my religious beliefs that my child not be educated with children of same-sex parents?” she asked.
Several conservatives focused instead on accommodating the schools.
“Why not seek the win/win?” Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked, pointing to roughly 2,000 participating preschools and 34 Catholic schools.
“There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 schools an appropriate fit for their children,” he said.
Related: Op-ed: A child’s access to preschool shouldn’t depend on who their parents love
Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton challenged the assumption that preschools are interchangeable.
“Think of the parent who needs a school that opens at 7:00 a.m. so she can get the bus that takes her to work,” she said.
Colorado seeks “equal opportunity, not some opportunity,” Norton said.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett questioned whether formally neutral conditions could nevertheless exclude religious institutions.
“If you know that the effect of choosing that requirement will push out those with a contrary belief, how is that different?” she asked.
Chief Justice John Roberts initially distinguished Colorado’s policy from explicit religious exclusions but later suggested their effects were “pretty much the same.”
Outside the court after the hearing, petitioner Lisa Sheley described the financial consequences for her family.
“All we wanted was for our little ones to have the same education we’ve chosen for their older siblings, but Colorado has punished us for that choice,” she said.
Reaves told reporters that families had paid thousands of dollars out of pocket and that enrollment at Catholic preschools in the archdiocese had fallen nearly 20 percent. He attributed two school closures to funding shortfalls and declining enrollment.
“It claimed that Catholic schools are the ones excluding families, even as Colorado excludes thousands of Catholic families,” Reaves said of the state’s argument.
LGBTQ+ advocates emphasized the children who could be denied admission. Lambda Legal and GLAD Law filed a brief supporting Colorado.
“No four-year-old should be turned away from a taxpayer-funded classroom because of who their parents are, including children of LGBTQ parents,” Lambda Legal attorney Karen Loewy said in a statement.
Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson likewise urged the court to uphold the requirements.
“Exclusion has no place in our educational system,” Robinson said.
A decision is expected by the end of June 2027. Reaves said outside the court that, if the schools prevail, he expects they could participate by the fall.

sources.text: A majority of the Supreme Court signalled on Tuesday it would allow Catholic preschools receiving taxpayer money to deny enrollment to children of same-sex couples, potentially delivering another significant win for religious rights in schools. The court’s conservative majority was unconvinced that a Colorado law, which bars discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender in publicly funded preschools, could be squared with recent high-profile precedents that expanded the ability of those religious schools to receive public money. Broadly, the case represents a clash between First Amendment religious protections and laws intended to protect gay and transgender Americans from discrimination. When those conflicts have come to the Supreme Court in recent years, religious claims have won time after time. And there was no indication over the course of two hours of an Election Day oral argument that the Colorado dispute would be any different. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, at one point, questioned why Colorado had “provoked” the confrontation and missed a “win-win” by enforcing the discrimination provision and not allowing Catholic schools to opt out to “respect religious rights.” “It seems like this is a would-be solution in search of a problem,” Kavanaugh, a member of the court’s conservative wing, told the Colorado attorney defending the state law. “I’m just trying to figure out why we’re here.” In many ways, though, the case was of the court’s own making. For years, the conservative majority has expanded the ability of religious schools to receive public funding — chipping away at a wall many Americans understood to have long separated church and state. But those decisions largely steered clear of questions about what would happen when those publicly funded religious schools declined to enroll the child of a gay couple or use a student’s preferred pronoun in the classroom. Sensing that Colorado’s argument was likely a lost cause, the court’s three-justice liberal wing repeatedly leaned into an attorney representing the Catholic parish and a Colorado family that sued to challenge the state’s anti-discrimination law. “What you’re basically saying is, ‘We can exclude people merely because the exposure to them would cause us harm’ — that’s really what you’re saying,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor told the attorney for the Trump administration, which opposes Colorado’s law. “That is completely what you’re saying: We can exclude children of same-sex marriage, we can exclude children who might have transgender feelings or beliefs because exposing other children to them creates a problem.” Sarah Harris, arguing for the Justice Department, rejected that framing. Instead, she said, the Catholic schools were exercising their religion by “requiring parents to agree with a school that they’re going to adhere to tenets of the Catholic faith and act consistently with them.” Colorado enacted a ballot provision in 2020 that provides state funding for a universal preschool program, allowing both public and private schools to take part. The program includes a nondiscrimination provision that requires each school receiving public money to provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll, regardless of race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity and other factors. The appeal, filed by the religious public interest firm Becket, appeared ready-made for a 6-3 conservative court that has repeatedly sided with religious interests. In one series of decisions, the court has made clear that when the government opens educational funding programs up to public and private schools, it cannot bar religious schools from taking part just because they are religious or offer religious instruction. The court in 2022, for instance, barred Maine from excluding religious schools from a tuition assistance program that allows parents to use vouchers to send their children to public or private schools. Maine responded to that decision by embracing language like Colorado’s, technically allowing religious schools to take part but imposing anti-discrimination language the Catholic Church says it cannot bear. Colorado’s history of cases involving religion and LGBTQ issues At least some conservative justices seemed frustrated with the idea that states could be using such anti-discrimination provisions as a pretext to bar religious participation. “If you know that the effect of choosing that requirement will push out those with contrary beliefs, how is that different?” conservative Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Colorado’s deputy solicitor general, Helen Norton. Norton said there is “zero evidence” that the state targeted religious schools with its anti-discrimination language. She noted the state encouraged religious schools to take part, and that some religious schools — including Catholic schools — were engaged in the program. And Colorado’s anti-discrimination provision, she said, was enacted before the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in the Maine case. A decision in the Colorado dispute is expected by the end of June. A few conservative justices noted that many claims pitting religious rights against LGBTQ Americans had come from Colorado in recent years. Supreme Court offers support for Catholic preschools challenging state funding requirements
The Supreme Court’s conservative majority offered clear support Tuesday for Catholic preschools that claim Colorado’s taxpayer-funded program improperly excludes them by unconstitutionally intruding on their religious rights.

It is the latest high-profile religious rights appeal to reach the high court in recent years, several of them originating from Colorado.

In a lively two-hour oral argument, the justices debated competing interests involving both religious liberty and a state’s interest in ensuring equal opportunity for gay and lesbian parents.
“I’m hard-pressed to think that, given those [Catholic] teachings, that any homosexual family is going to choose to go to one of these schools, but that should be their choice, not your choice to exclude them,” said Justice Sonia Sotomayor to the lawyer for the plaintiffs. “That’s what you’re asking for… You want an official statement by the State that I will subsidize you with public money even though – because I have a right to reject children.”

But Justice Brett Kavanaugh said the state’s motives, however well-intentioned, are promoting a kind of conformity that is not constitutionally permissible.

sources.news_title: The Supreme Court sounds eager to make you pay for anti-LGBTQ schools
sources.text:
There was one significant surprise during the Supreme Court’s Tuesday argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a case asking whether Colorado may require schools that accept state funding to treat LGBTQ families and students the same way they treat anyone else. For a brief moment, Chief Justice John Roberts seemed like he might break with his Republican colleagues and uphold Colorado’s policy.
The Supreme Court sounds eager to make you pay for anti-LGBTQ schools
At least five justices seem hostile to a law requiring taxpayer-funded schools to treat gay families the same as anyone else.
St. Mary arises out of a program that provides state-funded preschool to all Colorado children. Families are allowed to choose which school they wish their young child to attend, and private religious schools are eligible to participate in this program. But state law also prohibits any school that receives this funding from discriminating on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.
The plaintiffs include Catholic-identified schools that wish to exclude the children of same-sex couples, but that claim they should nonetheless be funded by Colorado’s taxpayers.
In recent years, the Court has followed a consistent pattern in cases that pit religious conservatives against LGBTQ Americans — religious conservatives always win. As several justices noted during Tuesday’s arguments, the Court’s legal doctrines governing these cases are incoherent and often seem to call for illogical results. But the pattern still holds. When a religious conservative seeks an exemption from a state or federal law that prohibits anti-LGBTQ discrimination, this Court gives them the exemption.
As Roberts pointed out early in the St. Mary argument, these plaintiffs are asking the Court to reach beyond its previous precedents. In Carson v. Makin (2022), the Court required Maine to include religious schools in a tuition voucher program that, under Maine law, only funded secular private schools. But Colorado’s program includes religious schools.
Colorado is perfectly willing to subsidize Catholic schools. It merely insists that those schools, like all other preschools in Colorado, must treat gay and trans people the same way they treat anyone else if they receive taxpayers’ money. If a Catholic school (or any other religious school, for that matter) does not wish to comply with this condition, it may still operate. It just won’t receive money from the state.
Yet, while Roberts’s first questions during Tuesday’s argument suggested that he might consider voting in favor of Colorado, none of his five Republican colleagues appeared open to that position (although Justice Amy Coney Barrett did ask some questions suggesting that she may hand Colorado a narrower loss than the Court’s right flank would prefer). And, by the end of the argument, even Roberts seemed sympathetic to the orthodox Republican position that, when LGBTQ rights conflict with religious conservatism, the religious party wins.
This suggests that soon, taxpayers will be required to fund discriminatory institutions, even in states where such discrimination is forbidden by law.
The two partisan factions on the Supreme Court live in completely different universes in religion cases
Roberts’s early question aside, one thing that was absolutely clear from Tuesday’s argument is that the Court’s Democratic minority and its Republican majority bring completely different values to the table in cases like St. Mary.
All three of the Court’s Democrats expressed concern that, if their Court doesn’t someday draw a line in the sand and say that religious conservatives do not receive literally any accommodation that they ask for in federal litigation, then that will lead to immoral results and prevent important American institutions from functioning.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, asked why, if religious schools are permitted to discriminate against gay people, aren’t they also allowed to discriminate against Black people? What if, for example, someone who sincerely believes that racial segregation is mandated by God opens up a school that excludes Black children?
Similarly, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson asked about a hypothetical school which teaches that only boys, and not girls, should be taught mathematics. Under the plaintiffs’ legal theory in St. Mary, why wouldn’t this school be entitled to an exemption from state laws requiring all schools to teach certain subjects, including math, to all students?
Meanwhile, Justice Elena Kagan asked deputy US solicitor general Sarah Harris (the Trump administration, naturally, supports the anti-LGBTQ side in St. Mary) whether ordinary public schools would be subject to a rule requiring states to accommodate the religious beliefs of anti-LGBTQ parents. When Harris indicated that they would, Kagan then asked why the parent of a public school student couldn’t demand that their child be educated in a different classroom than the children of same-sex parents — or demand some other accommodation that public schools would find it very difficult to provide?
But the Republican justices dismissed these concerns, with many of them suggesting that religious objectors may demand an exemption from nearly any law. The dominant view among the Court’s Republicans appeared to be that any law that imposes obligations on a religious conservative must survive a rigid legal rule known as “strict scrutiny,” the most skeptical level of review that courts apply in constitutional cases.
Nearly all government policies that are subjected to strict scrutiny fail, so, if strict scrutiny applies in cases like St. Mary, that would mean that religious conservatives nearly always prevail. Though, in fairness, Eric Rassbach, the plaintiffs’ lawyer in St. Mary, did suggest that a ban on race discrimination might be the rare law that can be enforced against religious schools. So, under the Republican justices’ approach, religious schools may not be allowed to exclude Black students. But they’d have free rein to violate many other laws.
With the exception of Roberts, the only Republican on the Court who seemed open to a more nuanced rule than simply applying strict scrutiny in every case was Barrett. And it’s not like Barrett was particularly sympathetic to the state.
Still, Barrett did float a way to decide this case that may be slightly narrower than many of her Republican colleagues’ views. Briefly, Barrett drew a distinction between a school that outright forbids the children of same-sex parents from attending, and a school that allows these children to attend, but only if the parents sign a statement denouncing homosexuality and agreeing to restrictions on their personal conduct — such as never appearing together at the school at the same time, so that no one can see that one of the school’s students has two parents of the same sex.
Barrett seemed to suggest that perhaps the Court could uphold Colorado’s ban on absolute exclusion, while simultaneously permitting religious schools to impose these humiliating obligations on same-sex families. As a practical matter, however, it is unclear how this rule would differ from one endorsing total exclusion of gay parents, because what parent would agree to these restrictions?
In any event, after Tuesday’s argument, it is hard to imagine the Court handing Colorado, or same-sex parents, anything that resembles a real win. Whether the Court endorses allowing schools to exclude same-sex parents entirely, or embraces something like Barrett’s rule, the practical result is likely to be the same. Religious conservatives get what they want; LGBTQ Americans must yield to the interests of those conservatives.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court appeared receptive Tuesday, Nov. 3, to arguments from Catholic preschools challenging Colorado’s requirement that schools receiving public education funding enroll children regardless of their or their parents’ sexual orientation or gender identity, raising the possibility of another significant ruling expanding constitutional protections for religious institutions.
The case, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, involves the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes and parents who contend that Colorado violated the First Amendment by excluding their preschools from the state’s universal preschool program because they require participating families to support Catholic teachings on marriage, sexuality and biological sex. The Trump administration supports the schools, arguing that government benefits cannot be conditioned on abandoning sincerely held religious practices.
According to Reuters’ coverage of Tuesday’s arguments, several conservative justices questioned whether Colorado’s policy effectively discriminates against religious institutions by imposing requirements those schools cannot accept without compromising their beliefs.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett challenged Colorado attorney Helen Norton to explain why attaching such conditions to a government benefit should be treated differently from directly excluding religious schools.
“Explain what the difference is between (explicit exclusion of religious schools) and then choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools will be unable to agree to?” Barrett asked.
Chief Justice John Roberts also questioned whether Colorado’s position conflicted with the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, which held that Maine could not exclude religious schools from a private-school tuition assistance program simply because they provided religious education.
“I think the effect of the law in Carson is pretty much the same as the effect of the law here. And we said in Carson that it turned on the substance of Free Exercise protections,” Roberts said. “And I wonder in what way you think this is different than Carson?”
The dispute centers on Colorado’s universal preschool program, which provides up to 15 hours of publicly funded preschool each week for eligible children during the year before kindergarten. The program was established following voter approval of a 2020 ballot initiative and allows parents to select participating public, private or religious schools.
Participating institutions must agree to provide equal enrollment opportunities regardless of several protected characteristics, including race, religion, sexual orientation and gender identity. Catholic schools are eligible to participate if they accept those conditions, but the plaintiffs maintain that their religious mission prevents them from agreeing to the requirements concerning sexual orientation and gender identity.
The Archdiocese of Denver and its affiliated schools argue that Colorado permits other participating preschools to establish enrollment preferences involving family income, disability status, siblings already attending the school and religious congregation membership. They contend that allowing those preferences while refusing religious accommodations creates unequal treatment under the First Amendment’s Free Exercise Clause.
Nicholas Reaves, representing the Catholic institutions, told the justices that religious instruction is fundamental to the schools’ purpose.
“To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the Church’s teachings,” Reaves said. “Because of this sincere religious exercise, the state has denied Colorado families the ability to use universal preschool funding at Catholic schools.”
The archdiocese oversees 34 Catholic preschools, and the plaintiffs say their enrollment has declined by approximately 20% since Colorado’s program began operating. They argue that excluding their institutions from the taxpayer-funded initiative places Catholic families at a financial disadvantage because parents must either pay for their preferred religious preschool or select another participating provider.
Colorado officials dispute that characterization, maintaining that the state does not exclude religious schools because of their faith. Instead, the state argues that every participating institution must follow the same nondiscrimination requirements when accepting public money.
“Colorado welcomes religious preschools to (the program). The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike,” Norton told the justices.
The state also maintains that Catholic preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including doctrines concerning marriage and sexuality, while participating in the program. According to Colorado’s attorneys, the dispute concerns whether publicly funded schools can deny enrollment based on protected characteristics rather than whether religious education itself is permissible.
“Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage, free to teach them while receiving public funding,” Norton said.
The court’s liberal justices challenged the argument that previous decisions protecting religious schools’ access to public funds necessarily require Colorado to waive conditions imposed on every participating institution.
Justice Elena Kagan distinguished between prohibiting discrimination against religious institutions and requiring a state to grant religious organizations exceptions unavailable to other providers.
“That’s not the principle that’s at issue here,” Kagan said. “The principle at issue here is: Do you have to treat them better?”
The legal dispute also involves the Supreme Court’s 1990 decision in Employment Division v. Smith, which generally permits neutral, broadly applicable laws that incidentally burden religious exercise. Colorado maintains that its preschool requirements satisfy that standard, while the Catholic plaintiffs argue that the state’s system of enrollment preferences undermines its claim that the rules are uniformly applicable.
A federal district court previously ruled against the Catholic institutions, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld that decision in September 2025. The appeals court concluded that Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirements were compatible with the First Amendment and that the state’s permitted enrollment preferences did not require an additional religious exemption.
The Supreme Court subsequently agreed to review the case, adding another religious liberty dispute to a series of decisions concerning government funding, religious institutions and protections against discrimination. As The Associated Press reported, the court has previously ruled in favor of religious schools challenging exclusions from publicly funded education programs in Maine and Montana, although the justices divided evenly in a separate 2025 case involving a proposed Catholic charter school in Oklahoma.
The ACLU of Colorado and other civil rights organizations have supported the state’s position, arguing that religious freedom does not require governments to finance institutions that refuse to comply with generally applicable nondiscrimination requirements. Supporters of the Catholic schools counter that public education benefits should remain available to families choosing religious education without forcing participating institutions to alter their admissions practices.
The justices did not issue a ruling Tuesday, and questions during oral arguments do not necessarily establish how individual members of the court will vote. A decision is expected by the end of June 2027.
The outcome could establish an important precedent for religious schools and other faith-based organizations seeking access to government programs while maintaining policies that conflict with state nondiscrimination requirements. A ruling favoring the Catholic preschools could expand the circumstances in which religious institutions qualify for exemptions, while a decision supporting Colorado would reinforce states’ authority to attach equal-access conditions to publicly funded services.

Supreme Court seems likely to side with Catholic preschools in fight over Colorado program
Washington — The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared likely to side with Catholic preschools challenging Colorado's refusal to exempt them from a nondiscrimination requirement and let them participate in its universal preschool program.
The nondiscrimination mandate at the center of the dispute, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, requires participating schools to provide children with an "equal opportunity" to enroll regardless of their race, religion, sexual orientation and gender identity, among other characteristics.
When Colorado was preparing to implement the program, the Archdiocese of Denver, which oversees 34 Catholic preschools, sought an exemption from the nondiscrimination rule, since they only enroll families that align with the Catholic Church's teachings, including on marriage, family and sexual identity.
The state, however, denied the request for an accommodation and said the Catholic schools could not "discriminate against children or families in violation of state statute."
The Archdiocese, two of its parishes and a family then sued the state, arguing that their exclusion from the universal preschool program violated the Constitution's Free Exercise Clause. Lower courts sided with the state and said the sexual orientation and gender identity provisions of the nondiscrimination rule are neutral and apply generally to providers participating in the universal preschool program.
But in arguments that spanned two hours on Tuesday, the court's conservative majority appeared likely to rule in favor of the Catholic preschools. Such a decision would join a line of recent rulings in which the Supreme Court, which has a 6-3 conservative majority, has sided with religious institutions challenging their exclusion from state benefits programs, opening the door for more public dollars to flow to religious schools.
Oral arguments
Several of the conservative justices repeatedly raised concerns that the nondiscrimination rule was effectively a back-door way to keep religious entities out of the universal preschool program.
"You agree, don't you, that Colorado could not say that Catholic schools or evangelical schools or Orthodox Jewish schools were excluded from participation in the UPK program?" Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Helen Norton, Colorado's deputy solicitor general. "Then explain what the difference is between that and choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools would be unable to agree to."
Barrett suggested the effect of the nondiscrimination requirement is to "push out" those with traditional beliefs.
"Why not seek the win-win?" Justice Brett Kavanaugh asked Norton about the state's refusal to exempt Catholic preschools. He noted that there are more than 2,000 preschools that participate in Colorado's universal preschool program, and only 34 are overseen by the Archdiocese of Denver.
"There are plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find among the 2,000 schools an appropriate fit for their children," he said.
Justice Samuel Alito raised Colorado's recent record of losses at the Supreme Court in religious liberty cases, in which the high court sided with a Christian baker, website designer and counselor.
"We have the state's record" in other First Amendment cases, Alito told Norton. "What should we make of this?"
But Norton, the Colorado deputy solicitor general, said Colorado "welcomes" religious preschools to its program.
"The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike," she said, adding that religious preschools can teach their beliefs on sex, gender or marriage and are "free to teach them while receiving public funding."
Nicholas Reaves, a lawyer with the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty who argued on behalf of the Archdiocese, said Colorado is denying Catholic preschools the ability to receive public benefits because of their religious exercise.
The three liberal justices each raised concerns that the Catholic schools were asking for a "special" accommodation from the state that would allow them to discriminate against families based on protected characteristics.
Justice Elena Kagan said that the principle the Supreme Court upheld in a 2022 case involving a Maine tuition-assistance program was that the state cannot treat religious institutions differently.
"That's not the principle that's at issue here," she said. "The principle at issue here is, do you have to treat them better?"
Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said the Archdiocese and its preschools are asking for a "special rule" that would allow them to turn away students based on their or their parents' sexual orientation or gender identity.
Colorado's universal preschool program launched after voters in the state approved a ballot measure in 2020 to provide state funding for a new program that intended to make preschool "widely available for free" to all 4-year-olds in the state.
Families are reimbursed for the cost of 15 hours of preschool per week, which amounts to more than $6,000 per year. The state uses a mixed-delivery system, meaning public, private, faith-based and secular preschools can participate. Those that do must sign a contract and meet state quality standards.
The statute that created the universal preschool program also imposed a nondiscrimination rule.
Colorado estimates there are roughly 40,000 children who are eligible for universal preschool across nearly 2,000 providers. The Archdiocese's 34 Catholic preschools do not participate in the program.

sources.news_title: Can schools take federal money and exclude LGBTQ+ families?
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. The case asks whether religious preschools that take taxpayer funds through Colorado’s Universal Preschool Program can deny enrollment to children because their parents are LGBTQ+.
Colorado offers free preschool to every family in the state through public and private providers, including religious schools. Providers that accept state funds, religious and secular alike, agree to give every family an equal opportunity to enroll.
Two parishes and the Archdiocese of Denver want the funding without that requirement, even though their schools never applied to take part in the program. They argue the rule violates their religious freedom. To receive state funds, they would be held to the same nondiscrimination rule as every other participating preschool. Both the federal district court and the Tenth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled for Colorado.
While some of the justices appeared ready to accept the petitioners’ invitation to upend the established framework for challenges to publicly funded programs by religious organizations, others clearly recognized the importance of Colorado’s commitment to ensuring that all state-funded preschools do not engage in discrimination against children with LGBTQ parents.
Lambda Legal and GLAD Law filed a friend-of-the-court brief supporting Colorado.
“When the state pays schools to provide preschool programming, the schoolhouse door must be open to every family. While religious schools can set their own admissions criteria when they are privately funded, every school, religious or secular, that chooses to take taxpayer dollars is barred from discriminating in violation of Colorado law,” said Karen Loewy, Senior Counsel and Director of Constitutional Law Practice at Lambda Legal. “No four-year-old should be turned away from a taxpayer-funded classroom because of who their parents are, including children of LGBTQ parents. Colorado’s requirements simply make sure public money isn’t used to discriminate, and the Constitution has long allowed states to set that condition.”
— David Taffet

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Skeptical of Colorado’s Preschool Nondiscrimination Rule for Religious Schools
sources.text:
The Supreme Court on Nov. 3 seemed sympathetic to arguments by Colorado Catholic preschools seeking to join the state’s universal preschool program while declining to enroll children based on sexual orientation or so-called gender identity—whether that of the child or the parents.
The case, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, asks whether Colorado can require Catholic preschools to follow its nondiscrimination rule on sexual orientation and gender identity if they want state preschool funding.
The schools argue that the rule clashes with the church’s religious beliefs and that the state already permits other exceptions.
Colorado says the rule is neutral and applies equally to every preschool taking public money, and that religious schools remain free to participate as long as they do not turn children away on those grounds. A ruling for the schools would make it harder for states to attach anti-discrimination conditions to public money that goes to religious schools. The Trump administration supports the Catholic schools in the case.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit affirmed, also citing Smith. It held that Carson v. Makin (2022) and related cases did not apply because Colorado’s rule did not explicitly exclude religious schools. The court also concluded that the program’s various exceptions and preferences did not undermine the general applicability of the rule, so the requirement was subject to a less demanding form of constitutional scrutiny known as rational basis review. In Carson, the Supreme Court held that Maine couldn’t exclude religious schools from a tuition assistance program simply because they’re religious.
“Explain what the difference is between [explicitly excluding religious schools] and then choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools will be unable to agree to,” Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Helen Norton, Colorado’s deputy solicitor general.
Norton said the state welcomes religious preschools but requires that they meet the same equal opportunity conditions as every other public or private preschool.
Justice Samuel Alito listed three First Amendment religion cases from recent years in which the Supreme Court struck down Colorado laws for interfering with religious freedom.
The justice asked Norton, “What should we make of all of this?”
Justice Brett Kavanaugh followed up by pointing out that there are 2,000 participating schools and only 34 of them are Catholic.
He asked Norton why Colorado had “provoked” a confrontation, when there was a “win-win” available. The justice pointed to the program’s other enrollment preferences—such as allowing schools to prioritize children of single parents, or those interested in STEM or vegetarian diets—and asked why religious schools couldn’t receive similar flexibility.
“It seems like this is … a would-be solution in search of a problem. And I’m just trying to figure out … why we’re here,” Kavanaugh said.
Conservative justices questioned why Colorado needed to condition funding for the program on an equal opportunity mandate, as they raised concerns about nondiscrimination laws being used in an indirect way to discriminate against religious beliefs.
“When a state imposes a condition that it knows certain religions cannot accept, the only question that is presented is whether that was done with the intent to discriminate against those religions,” Alito said.
Liberal justices framed the case as one that could open the door to discrimination.
“What you’re basically saying is we can exclude people merely because of exposure to them,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor said to Principal Deputy U.S. Solicitor General Sarah Harris.
“We can exclude children of same-sex marriage,” the justice said. “We can exclude children who might … have transgender feelings or beliefs because exposing other children to them creates a problem.”
The Supreme Court is expected to rule on the case by June or July 2027.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Sympathetic to Catholic Schools in Funding Fight
sources.text:
The US Supreme Court appeared likely to side with Catholic parishes seeking a religious exemption to state nondiscrimination law they say excludes them from Colorado’s universal preschool program because of their beliefs about gender and sexuality.
The justices heard argument Tuesday over the program, which is open to any preschool provider in the state that offers equal enrollment opportunities to all children.
The Archdiocese of Denver and two nearby parishes argue the nondiscrimination requirement violates the First Amendment by requiring them to admit students whose families don’t adhere to church teachings on gender identity and sexual orientation.
Chief Justice John Roberts seemed concerned about the limits to the principle the Catholic parishes are pushing for, but also said the effect of Colorado’s law looked “pretty much the same” as a Maine law excluding religious schools from a public tuition assistance program the court struck down in 2022 in Carson v. Makin.
The conservative-dominated court has viewed state efforts to block religious schools from public dollars with increasing skepticism.
Carson was the third in a line of cases in which the court has found efforts to carve religious institutions out of public subsidies violate the Free Exercise Clause.
Conservative justices largely appeared to open to ruling against Colorado, even at times invoking the state’s dismal track record before the justices in recent years on cases tied to religious beliefs.
Justice Samuel Alito at one point ran through that tally of cases as he asked why Colorado wouldn’t have been on notice as to why its equal-opportunity mandate might clash with court precedent.
The cases include Chiles v. Salazar, in which the court last March ruled for a Christian counselor who claimed a First Amendment right to engage in talk therapy aimed at changing a child’s sexual orientation or gender identity.
Justices Amy Coney Barrett and Brett Kavanaugh also seemed to question why Colorado fought all the way to the Supreme Court, suggesting they could’ve instead reached a resolution that allows parents to take their children to schools of their choice.
“Is there any record of those same-sex parents trying to attend these Catholic preschools and being turned away?” Barrett asked. She also distinguished this dispute from past court cases that turned on efforts to combat discrimination.
Helen Norton, a deputy solicitor general for Colorado, argued that states retain strong and longstanding interests “to ensure that they invest their public funds in entities that do not deny equal opportunity.”
The court’s liberal bloc were more skeptical toward the parishes’ arguments, saying their view on the law would invite even more requests for religious opt outs.
“Your bottom line is your school can reject a child because their parents are homosexual,” said Justice Sonia Sotomayor, asking what’s to stop groups from offering a religious defense against serving children of Black parents.
“It seems to me you’re asking for a special rule for religious schools,” Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said.
Avoiding Smith
The court declined to use the case as an opportunity to reconsider its landmark 1990 ruling in Employment Division v. Smith, although the parishes and several conservative justices appeared eager to distinguish public benefit cases from the holding.
In Smith, the court held incidental infringement on religious practice was permissible under the First Amendment by neutral, generally applicable laws. Both a district court and the US Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit upheld Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement under Smith.
Arguing for Colorado, Norton said the state viewed the court’s Carson line of cases as implementations of Smith. That drew pushback from Alito and Justice Clarence Thomas, who noted the court didn’t even cite Smith in two of them.
“Why would we do so here?” Thomas asked.
Nicholas Reaves, an attorney for the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty representing the parishes, argued even Smith — an opinion several of the court’s conservatives, including Thomas and Alito, have called to overturn — distinguished cases where the government was seeking to withhold benefits rather than enforce criminal laws.
“If someone is differently situation because of their religious beliefs, an accommodation is neutrality,” Reaves said.
The Trump administration supported the parishes’ position. US Solicitor General John Sauer’s office filed a rare unsolicited brief urging the justices to take up the case, and argued Tuesday on the side of the schools.
A decision is expected by the end of the court’s term in late June or early July.
The case is St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, U.S., No. 25-581, argued on 11/3/26.

Justices Appear to Side with Catholic Schools in Colorado Pre-K Admissions Case
sources.text:
Justices Appear to Side with Catholic Schools in Colorado Pre-K Admissions Case
The case is the fourth from Colorado since 2018 that attempts to balance laws protecting the rights of LGBTQ people against religious exercise.
Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter
The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared skeptical of a Colorado law that requires state-funded pre-K programs to accept children from LGBTQ families even if it conflicts with their religious beliefs.
For two hours, the justices debated a case that could take the court a step further in protecting religious freedom, with the conservative majority suggesting that the state should allow Catholic pre-K programs to deny admission to children with same-sex parents.
Helen Norton, the attorney who argued the state’s side, said officials aimed to make preschool widely available to religious families and that providers “remain free to teach their religious beliefs … about sex or gender or marriage,” as long as they adhere to the state’s nondiscrimination law. Some LGBTQ families, she said, might even prefer a nearby Catholic preschool, despite their teachings, because it better accommodates their schedules.
But Justice Brett Kavanaugh, one of the six conservatives on the court, said there’s a way to “avoid the clash.”
“Why not seek the win-win?” he asked, by exempting the religious schools from the rule and allowing LGBTQ parents to choose from any of the other 2,000 available programs.
Because the state allows admission preferences for low-income students and kids with disabilities, it can’t close the door on schools that “exist to pass on the faith to the next generation,” said Nicholas Reaves, senior counsel at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty and the lead attorney for the parents and preschools. Colorado’s mandate accommodates “important secular interests,” he said, but considers its law “a hard limit when petitioners sought a religious accommodation.”
The case, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, is the latest in an increasing number of cases before the court that weigh the interests of religion against rules the government says should apply to everyone. It’s also the fourth major First Amendment case from Colorado since 2018 dealing with religious exercise. They include a 2018 case in which a baker refused to make a case for a same-sex couple and a challenge last year to a law banning conversion therapy for transgender minors. The court has ruled against the state in all three cases, and one observer doesn’t expect this case to turn out any differently.
“Colorado keeps losing,” said Elliot Regenstein, a partner with Foresight Law + Policy, a Washington, D.C.-based firm focused on education. “This court has been very sympathetic to free exercise rights.”
But Elena Kagan, one of the three liberals on the court, said siding with the preschools would make it even easier for religious groups and individuals to continue to claim that a generally applicable law creates a “substantial burden” on their religious freedoms.
“Why would we put ourselves in the middle of that in all these cases?” she asked. “With respect to public schools alone, these inquiries could go on forever.”
‘Asking for special treatment’
Much of the exchange between the justices and the attorneys focused on which court precedent is most relevant in this case. Colorado officials have leaned heavily on Employment Division v. Smith, a 1990 opinion in which the justices said one’s religious beliefs don’t exempt a person from complying with a law that applies to everyone.
Both Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Clarence Thomas repeatedly asked the attorneys how this case is different from Carson v. Makin, in which the court said states can’t exclude faith-based schools from choice programs because they practice religion.
In that case, the “court was concerned about treating religious entities worse than everybody else,” said Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, one of the liberals. But here, the preschools, she said, are asking for special treatment.
“Your school wants to discriminate by exclusion,” she said. “Nobody else is allowed to do that.”
Advocates for LGBTQ students fear a ruling against the state could have negative consequences for all types of families.
“Parents already struggle to find affordable and accessible preschools that work for their family,” said Brian Dittmeier, the director of LGBTQI+ Equality at the National Women’s Law Center. “A ruling that gives license to discriminate could also lead to other family structures being discriminated against in publicly funded programs, including households headed by single mothers, divorced parents and interfaith couples.”
Regenstein, with Foresight, said the court could turn to a third case to decide the outcome — Fulton v. City of Philadelphia. In that opinion, the court unanimously held in 2021 that a Catholic social service agency had a right to exclude same-sex couples from becoming foster parents. In the ruling, Roberts wrote that the nondiscrimination rule didn’t apply to everyone because exceptions were already allowed at the discretion of city officials.
“I don’t think you need to say anything more than you already said in Fulton,” said Reaves, the attorney for the preschools.
Roberts tends to prefer narrow rulings and may go in that direction, said Ryan Gardner, senior counsel at First Liberty Institute, a conservative law firm that represents a Maine church that is suing the state over a nondiscrimination rule similar to Colorado’s. A broader opinion would say that the Smith ruling, which dealt with a law against drug use, never applies to public benefit programs like universal preschool.
Implications for pre-K
However the court rules, the outcome could have significant implications for state preschool programs, Regenstein said. Most states already run their pre-K programs through a mixture of schools and private providers. Some, like Hawaii and California, even have more than one program, allowing a place for faith-based providers.
If the justices side with Colorado, any existing regulations that apply to faith-based providers will remain constitutional, Regenstein and his colleagues explained in an analysis prior to Tuesday’s arguments.
But if the Catholic preschools and the families prevail, states would have to make some decisions about whether to allow faith-based providers to participate on their own terms or rethink whether they include private programs at all. They could, for example, only allow state-funded pre-K programs to operate out of public schools. But such a policy would inevitably spark litigation claiming religious discrimination, they wrote.
“There haven’t been that many high-profile cases about preschools,” he said. “We may be entering an era where in some states, litigation just becomes a part of life for the next few years.”

US Supreme Court Leans Toward Catholic Schools in Clash Over Pre-K Funding
A majority of U.S. Supreme Court justices sounded ready to require that Colorado provide Catholic schools government funding for preschool even if the schools refuse to guarantee admission for children of same-sex couples, during oral arguments Tuesday in a case involving a school in the Archdiocese of Denver.
The case, St. Mary School v. Roy, centers on a preschool-through-grade-8 Catholic school in Littleton that wants to participate in the state’s universal preschool program.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a member of the court’s conservative majority, described the case as a clash between the free exercise of religion and the right to same-sex marriage the court found in Obergefell v. Hodges in 2015. But he suggested the clash is unnecessary because parents in Colorado have so many options for prekindergarten, since there are more than 2,000 providers in the state, while the Archdiocese of Denver has only 34 schools that provide the service.
“Why has this been provoked when there’s an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school, that’s a fit for them, and to respect religious rights?” he asked.
Helen Norton, deputy solicitor general for the state of Colorado, said parents often choose prekindergarten programs based on their location and their hours rather than their curriculum.
“Colorado has an interest in ensuring that its public funds go to schools that ensure equal opportunity — not some opportunity, that ensure equal opportunity to public-funded options, regardless of protected-class status,” Norton said, replying to Kavanaugh’s question. “Families are harmed when they’re turned away from the publicly funded school that makes their lives work because of their protected-class status.”
‘Creating a Catholic Community’
In 2020, Colorado voters approved a state-funded universal prekindergarten program, using increases in tobacco-related taxes to pay for it. The state government is planning to spend about $360 million for the program during the 2026-2027 school year. The state pays preschool providers about $6,100 per year for 15 hours a week of instruction for 4-year-olds during the 2026-2027 school year, according to state standards.
Catholic schools want to participate in the program, but the Archdiocese of Denver objects to a state mandate concerning admissions.
A Colorado state statute requires that preschools participating in the funding program provide children “an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services” regardless of eight protected classes — including “sexual orientation” and “gender identity” — “as such characteristics and circumstances apply to the child or the child’s family.”
A lawyer for the Catholic schools told justices Tuesday that Church and school officials want to make admissions decisions on a case-by-case basis in alignment with Catholic teachings instead of simply allowing all comers because of a state mandate.
“I think it’s their thoughtful attempt to say, ‘We’re creating a Catholic community,’” said Nicholas Reaves, senior counsel for the Becket law group, which is representing the Catholic schools.
Reaves got hostile questions from the court’s three liberals (Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson) and either friendly or neutral questions from the court’s five conservatives (Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett), which suggests how the decision might ultimately go. (The chief justice, John Roberts, often seen as a swing vote, mostly moderated the discussion.)
Sarah Harris, principal deputy solicitor general in the Trump administration, also argued on the Catholic schools’ side during oral presentations Tuesday.
Many Options
The history of Catholic schools in the 19th century came up during oral arguments, including their origin in concerns among Catholic clerics and parents that government-run public schools were providing a Protestant point of view to the exclusion of Catholicism. Justice Kavanaugh, a Catholic, at one point asked the lawyer for the state of Colorado about a moment in the trial record when the administrator of the state’s universal prekindergarten program was asked about Catholic history.
“The director of the program, by all accounts a dutiful public servant, … was asked at the trial, ‘Are you aware that Catholics have historically been discriminated against?’ And she answered, ‘No,’” Kavanaugh said. “I was surprised by that answer and curious if that’s Colorado’s position.”
“Not at all, Your Honor,” Norton replied. “And it’s Colorado’s position that the equal-opportunity requirements help religious families. They ensure that Catholic families are not turned away from the UPK [universal prekindergarten] school that best meets their needs because of their faith or because of any other protected characteristic. And a history of discrimination against Catholics is among the reasons that requirement is so important.”
Some legal observers have suggested that a majority of the U.S. Supreme Court may use the Colorado case as a vehicle to overturn the Smith decision in 1990, which, although written by the late conservative Justice Antonin Scalia, is disliked by many religious-liberty advocates who argue it doesn’t respect free-exercise rights enough.
Yet the lawyer representing the Catholic schools on Tuesday offered narrower grounds for the justices to overturn Colorado’s admissions requirements, noting that for every Catholic preschool program in the Archdiocese of Denver, there are two universal prekindergarten programs already in the state’s program within 3 miles of it.
Said Reaves, “This is just not really a problem in real life.”

AP — The Trump administration joined the Archdiocese of Denver on Tuesday in urging the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling allowing a state-funded preschool program in Colorado to exclude Roman Catholic schools that don’t comply with equal-opportunity requirements — the latest religious-rights case before the conservative-majority court.
