Written by conservative icon Justice Antonin Scalia in a case over the spiritual use of peyote, a cactus containing mescaline that’s sacred to many Indigenous people, the decision has nevertheless long been a target of the conservative legal movement.
The Denver archdiocese argues that it’s unconstitutional to exclude Catholic preschools from the state’s program over their admissions policy for LGBTQ+ families. The Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday on the archdiocese’s request to overturn a 10th Circuit decision in the state’s favor.
Colorado, meanwhile, says the refusal to admit kids from those families would violate the state’s anti-discrimination law.
But St. Mary Catholic Parish and the Archdiocese of Denver argue that the policy is based on religious teachings about same-sex marriage and that excluding them violates their free-exercise rights.
Nicholas Reaves, an attorney for the archdiocese and two parish preschools, said allowing Catholic schools to participate in Colorado’s publicly funded preschools program “will create more seats for everyone, even for families who disagree with Catholic teachings.”
“This is not a zero-sum game,” Reaves said. “Letting families use universal preschool funding at Catholic schools won’t take away a single seat from the over 2,000 preschools already participating in the program.”
President Donald Trump’s administration is supporting the Catholic institutions. Justice Elena Kagan, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama, said the administration seems to be arguing that children of same-sex marriage can be excluded because “exposing” them to other students “creates a problem.”
“We have a clear line now and you want us to just upend it in one particular area of law,” Kagan told Justice Department attorney Sarah Harris.
“No, I think the court currently has a mess,” Harris said.
In the Colorado case, the high court could be sympathetic to the schools. The justices have sided with religious schools in similar disputes before, ruling in recent years that they can’t be excluded from programs in Maine and Montana that provide public aid to private schools. In 2025, though, the court deadlocked over a plan to establish a publicly funded Catholic charter school after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself.
The Colorado universal preschool program was created by a 2020 ballot measure. It provides public funding for preschool at schools chosen by parents.
The plaintiffs, represented by the group Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, say the state has allowed other preschools to prioritize children with disabilities or those from low-income families, so admission based on religious beliefs about gender and same-sex marriage should be allowed, too. The Catholic preschools say their enrollment has dropped 20% since the program started.
Colorado argues that the other admissions decisions are in line with the state’s anti-discrimination rules.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor, who was nominated to the court by Democratic President Barack Obama, asked Reaves if the Catholic school can reject a child simply because their parents are a same-sex couple.
“Is that the bottom line?” she asked.
“If it’s the sincere religious exercise of the petitioner, then I think that would be permitted,” Reaves said.
Helen Norton, an attorney for the state, said Colorado is “neutral toward religion” and welcomes religious preschools to participate in the program — provided that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet.
“Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage,” Norton said. “But families have no right to change a school’s curriculum.”
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was nominated to the court by Trump, a Republican, suggested Colorado’s law has created an unnecessary “clash of rights” between LGBTQ+ families and “religious believers.”
“Just trying to figure out why we’re here,” Kavanaugh told Norton. ”Why has this been provoked when there’s an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school that’s a fit for them, and respect religious rights?”
Norton said preschools aren’t “interchangeable” for parents and children.
“Families are harmed when they’re turned away from the publicly funded school that makes their lives work because of the protected class status,” she said.

US Supreme Court seen siding with Catholic schools denied state funding
Washington (United States) (AFP) – Conservatives who dominate the US Supreme Court appeared Tuesday to support a challenge by two Catholic preschools to a state requirement that they enroll children of gay or transgender parents in order to receive public funds.
Issued on:
The court, with six conservative judges to three liberals, has in recent years backed expanding the presence of religion in public life in America and has been keen to protect religious freedom, particularly in schools.
This current case involves Colorado, which provides state funding for tuition at public or private preschools, including faith-based institutions.
But Colorado has withheld money from the Catholic preschools involved in this case for violating anti-discrimination laws because they bar children of gay or transgender parents.
In a filing with the Supreme Court prior to Tuesday's hearing, Colorado said participants in the preschool funding program must enroll children regardless of the race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity of the child or their parents.
The Catholic Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes and two parents, Dan and Lisa Sheley, filed a lawsuit seeking a religious exemption. But they lost in lower courts, prompting the appeal to the nation's highest court.
President Donald Trump's administration has backed the Catholic plaintiffs, who cite the First Amendment to the US Constitution guaranteeing freedom of religion.
Colorado welcomes religious preschools to the funding program, Helen Norton, the state's deputy solicitor general, told the court.
"The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike," Norton said.
But conservative justices seemed to challenge the state, saying Colorado failed to acknowledge that its non-discrimination requirements and some religious beliefs could be incompatible.
Judge Amy Coney Barrett asked Norton to explain, for instance, the difference between explicitly excluding religious schools from funding and "choosing to impose a condition that you know that those schools will be unable to agree to."
One of court's liberal judges, Elena Kagan, said the plaintiffs were seeking not equal rights but rather preferential treatment.
"They need to be treated differently from other people -- because of their religious faith, to have a special accommodation," Kagan said.
Nicholas Reaves, a lawyer the Catholic plaintiffs, argued that "if someone is different, differently situated because of their religion," the way to remain neutral is to grant them an accommodation.
The Supreme Court, which includes three justices nominated by Trump, has sided with religious-right claims in a number of high-profile cases, several of which have involved Colorado.
In 2018, the court ruled in favor of a Colorado baker who declined to make a wedding cake for a same-sex couple, and more recently the court backed a Christian therapist who challenged a Colorado law banning "conversion therapy" for LGBTQ minors.
The Supreme Court is expected to issue a ruling in the preschools case by June 2027.

sources.news_title: Conservative justices likely to endorse Catholic preschool exclusion of LGBTQ families
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (CN) — The Supreme Court’s conservative supermajority seemed likely Tuesday to give anti-LGBTQ Catholic preschools a path around Colorado’s requirement that taxpayer dollars only go to schools that are open to all.
During two hours of oral arguments, the Republican appointees dismissed Colorado’s need to condition funding for its universal preschool program on an equal opportunity mandate, and they elevated concerns that nondiscrimination laws could be used to indirectly discriminate against religious beliefs.
“When a state imposes a condition that it knows certain religions cannot accept, the only question that is presented is whether that was done with the intent to discriminate against those religions,” Justice Samuel Alito, a George W. Bush appointee, said.
St. Mary Catholic Parish says it was excluded from the Centennial State’s universal preschool program because it is only open to families that are supportive of the Catholic Church’s teaching on sex and marriage. The preschool filed a lawsuit in 2023 after being denied a religious exemption from Colorado’s equal opportunity mandate.
Two lower courts dismissed the suit, finding Colorado’s program did not explicitly discriminate based on religion. But the high court appeared likely to reverse, viewing the case in line with the Roberts court’s recent First Amendment jurisprudence.
In Trinity Lutheran v. Comer in 2017, the court held churches couldn’t be excluded from secular aid programs. Then, in 2020’s Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, the justices ruled states couldn’t refuse government aid to schools controlled by churches.
Those two rulings culminated in the Supreme Court’s landmark 2022 ruling in Carson v. Makin, holding state-funded school choice programs must include education at religious institutions.
Chief Justice John Roberts, another George W. Bush appointee, said the effect of the law in Carson was the same in St. Mary’s case, preventing schools from receiving funding based on their religious beliefs.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett, a Donald Trump appointee, questioned why Colorado couldn’t have foreseen its mandate being a problem when the high court has repeatedly ruled against the state’s protections for LGBTQ rights in cases concerning cakemakers, website designers and conversion therapy.
Justice Neil Gorsuch, also a Trump appointee, further suggested states have intentionally enacted similar laws to Colorado’s to circumvent the court’s protections of religious beliefs.
The liberal wing had starkly different views on the case before the high court. All three Democratic appointees framed the matter as an attempt to greenlight discrimination against LGBTQ families.
“What you’re basically saying is we can exclude people merely because of exposure to them,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor, a Barack Obama appointee, said. “We can exclude children of same-sex marriage. We can exclude children who might have transgender feelings or beliefs because exposing other children to them creates a problem.”
Sotomayor and the other liberal justices said excluding LGBTQ families was no different than using religious beliefs as justification for discriminating based on race.
“There’s no principled basis, I think, to distinguish between an entity that says my religious faith says my children can’t go to school with the children of gay people from a religious entity that says my religion says my children can’t go to school with the children of Black people,” Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a Joe Biden appointee, said.
Instead of equal treatment, the liberal justices framed St. Mary’s case as a request for special treatment. As such, Justice Elena Kagan, another Obama appointee, said it was “far-fetched” to suggest that Colorado was surreptitiously targeting religious beliefs.
St. Mary’s case asked the justices to apply strict scrutiny to public funding requirements that interfere with protected rights. But Kagan questioned why the high court would want to put itself in the middle of weighing the importance of religious beliefs versus nondiscrimination interests of the state in an endless number of cases.
The conservative justices appeared undeterred by their colleagues’ concerns. Gorsuch remarked that he struggled to see how applying strict scrutiny would “be the end of the world,” and Justice Brett Kavanaugh, another Trump appointee, noted the court’s support for LGBTQ rights wasn’t in spite of other rights.
“One of the things that Obergefell was very careful to say, though, was that in recognizing a constitutional right to same-sex marriage, that the court was also respecting the rights of people, particularly religious people, who had religious beliefs that were different, and that it was important going forward as a country to make sure both rights were respected,” Kavanaugh said.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court appears to favor Catholic preschools in clash over LGBTQ, religious rights
Supreme Court leans toward Catholic preschools in fight over LGBTQ+ protections
U.S. Supreme Court leans toward Catholic schools in clash over pre-K funding
sources.text:
A majority of U.S. Supreme Court justices sounded ready to require that Colorado provide Catholic schools government funding for preschool even if the schools refuse to guarantee admission for children of same-sex couples, during oral arguments Tuesday in a case involving a school in the Archdiocese of Denver.
The case, St. Mary School v. Roy, centers on a preschool-through-grade-8 Catholic school in Littleton that wants to participate in the state’s universal preschool program.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a member of the court’s conservative majority, described the case as a clash between the free exercise of religion and the right to same-sex marriage the court found in Obergefell v. Hodges in 2015. But he suggested the clash is unnecessary because parents in Colorado have so many options for prekindergarten, since there are more than 2,000 providers in the state, while the Archdiocese of Denver has only 34 schools that provide the service.
“Why has this been provoked when there’s an ability for everyone to go to the school, a good school, that’s a fit for them, and to respect religious rights?” he asked.
Helen Norton, deputy solicitor general for the state of Colorado, said parents often choose prekindergarten programs based on their location and their hours rather than their curriculum.
“Colorado has an interest in ensuring that its public funds go to schools that ensure equal opportunity — not some opportunity, that ensure equal opportunity to public-funded options, regardless of protected-class status,” Norton said, replying to Kavanaugh’s question. “Families are harmed when they’re turned away from the publicly funded school that makes their lives work because of their protected-class status.”
‘Creating a Catholic community’
In 2020, Colorado voters approved a state-funded universal prekindergarten program, using increases in tobacco-related taxes to pay for it. The state government is planning to spend about $360 million for the program during the 2026-2027 school year. The state pays preschool providers about $6,100 per year for 15 hours a week of instruction for 4-year-olds during the 2026-2027 school year, according to state standards.
Catholic schools want to participate in the program, but the Archdiocese of Denver objects to a state mandate concerning admissions.
A Colorado state statute requires that preschools participating in the funding program provide children “an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services” regardless of eight protected classes — including “sexual orientation” and “gender identity” — “as such characteristics and circumstances apply to the child or the child’s family.”
A lawyer for the Catholic schools told justices Tuesday that Church and school officials want to make admissions decisions on a case-by-case basis in alignment with Catholic teachings instead of simply allowing all comers because of a state mandate.
“I think it’s their thoughtful attempt to say, ‘We’re creating a Catholic community,’” said Nicholas Reaves, senior counsel for the Becket law group, which is representing the Catholic schools.
Reaves got hostile questions from the court’s three liberals (Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson) and either friendly or neutral questions from the court’s five conservatives (Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett), which suggests how the decision might ultimately go. (The chief justice, John Roberts, often seen as a swing vote, mostly moderated the discussion.)
Sarah Harris, principal deputy solicitor general in the Trump administration, also argued on the Catholic schools’ side during oral presentations Tuesday.
Many options
The history of Catholic schools in the 19th century came up during oral arguments, including their origin in concerns among Catholic clerics and parents that government-run public schools were providing a Protestant point of view to the exclusion of Catholicism. Kavanaugh, a Catholic, at one point asked the lawyer for the state of Colorado about a moment in the trial record when the administrator of the state’s universal prekindergarten program was asked about Catholic history.
“The director of the program, by all accounts a dutiful public servant, … was asked at the trial, ‘Are you aware that Catholics have historically been discriminated against?’ And she answered, ‘No,’” Kavanaugh said. “I was surprised by that answer and curious if that’s Colorado’s position.”
“Not at all, Your Honor,” Norton replied. “And it’s Colorado’s position that the equal-opportunity requirements help religious families. They ensure that Catholic families are not turned away from the UPK [universal prekindergarten] school that best meets their needs because of their faith or because of any other protected characteristic. And a history of discrimination against Catholics is among the reasons that requirement is so important.”
Some legal observers have suggested that a majority of the U.S. Supreme Court may use the Colorado case as a vehicle to overturn the Smith decision in 1990, which, although written by the late conservative Justice Antonin Scalia, is disliked by many religious-liberty advocates who argue it doesn’t respect free-exercise rights enough.
Yet the lawyer representing the Catholic schools on Tuesday offered narrower grounds for the justices to overturn Colorado’s admissions requirements, noting that for every Catholic preschool program in the Archdiocese of Denver, there are two universal prekindergarten programs already in the state’s program within three miles of it.
Said Reaves: “This is just not really a problem in real life.”
This story was first published by the National Catholic Register, the sister partner of EWTN News, and has been adapted by EWTN News.

Supreme Court hears clash between Catholic preschools, Colorado over ‘universal’ program
WASHINGTON (OSV News) — The U.S. Supreme Court heard oral arguments Nov. 3 in a case over a clash between Catholic preschools and the state of Colorado over whether those schools can participate in the state’s universal preschool program.
The program provides funds — up to about $6,000 — to parents to send their child to the preschool of their choice, public or private, including faith-based schools.
Two Catholic parishes with preschools in the Archdiocese of Denver have alleged the state of Colorado excluded the religious preschools from participating in the program due to their religious beliefs. The schools require faculty and parents to sign a “statement of community beliefs” acknowledging the Catholic Church’s teachings on topics including marriage, sexuality and gender.
But Colorado has argued the Catholic preschools ran afoul of a nondiscrimination rule in the program that prohibits participating schools from refusing admission to any child on the basis of the sexual orientation and gender identity of the child or the child’s family.
“The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation,” Nicholas Reaves, senior counsel at Becket, a religious liberty law firm representing the schools, said during oral arguments. “To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the Church’s teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the state has denied Colorado families the ability to use universal preschool funding at Catholic schools.”
Basis of opposition to Colorado policy questioned
Justice Sonia Sotomayor pressed Reaves, arguing, “The Catholic schools are not being excluded on their face. They’re choosing not to participate, because they won’t get an exemption.”
“For the Catholic Church, it’s not about excluding anyone based on who they are,” he replied.
Sotomayor continued, “They’re saying we’ll exclude your children, if their parents are homosexual.”
Reaves said, “All families, regardless of who they are, even if they’re Catholic, have to agree to the statement of community beliefs in good faith. That’s the requirement.”
According to the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith’s 2024 declaration, “Dignitas Infinita” (“Infinite Dignity”), the Catholic Church holds “that every person, regardless of sexual orientation, ought to be respected in his or her dignity and treated with consideration, while ‘every sign of unjust discrimination’ is to be carefully avoided,” but opposes what it calls “gender theory.” The teaching document described sexual difference as “the greatest possible difference that exists between living beings,” which in humans “becomes the source of that miracle that never ceases to surprise us: the arrival of new human beings in the world.”
Justices question lawfulness of Colorado policy
Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton argued that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools” to the program, sometimes called UPK.
“The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike. UPK is neutral towards religion,” Norton said.
Justice Brett Kavanaugh questioned Norton on whether Colorado’s position was consistent with allowing single-sex preschools to participate in the program. Norton replied that biological sex is “not one of the characteristics enumerated in the UPK law.”
But more justices appeared inclined toward the preschools’ position. Chief Justice John Roberts remarked the effect of Colorado’s law seemed “pretty much the same” as a Maine law the court struck down in its 2022 Carson v. Makin decision. The court found that law improperly excluded religious schools from a public tuition assistance program.
Supreme Court to decide by next June
Kelley Robinson, president of the Human Rights Campaign, an LGBTQ+ advocacy group, argued in a Nov. 3 statement that the case “is straightforward — schools receiving public funds from a state universal preschool program cannot be allowed to use taxpayer dollars to leave LGBTQ+ families behind.”
“As the arguments made clear today, Colorado’s non-discrimination requirement ensures no family can be denied a quality education simply for who they are — it is lawful and should be upheld. Exclusion has no place in our educational system,” Robinson said.
During a brief press conference after oral arguments, Reaves likened Colorado’s position to a “‘no Catholics need apply’ policy.”
Colorado, he said, “argued that Catholic schools must abandon their religious exercise to participate in a program open to everyone else. It claimed that Catholic schools are the ones excluding families, even as Colorado excludes thousands of Catholic families, and it insisted with a straight face that a program can still be universal while shutting out families for their faith.”
Oral arguments took place the same day as the Nov. 3 elections.
A decision in the case is expected by the end of the Supreme Court’s term, which typically ends in June.
Kate Scanlon is a national reporter for OSV News covering Washington. Follow her on X @kgscanlon.

sources.news_title: St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy: What the Justices Said
sources.text:
The Supreme Court’s conservative justices appeared sympathetic on Tuesday, Nov. 3, to Catholic preschools fighting Colorado’s universal pre-K rules in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, Reuters reported. Colorado makes participating schools give kids an equal shot at a seat, whatever the sexual orientation or gender identity of the child or parents.
Justice Sonia Sotomayor, one of the court’s three liberals, was skeptical. “What you’re basically saying is, we can exclude people merely because exposure to them would cause us harm,” she told Sarah M. Harris, the Justice Department lawyer supporting the parishes, Reuters reported.
Justice Elena Kagan told Nicholas Reaves, the Becket lawyer arguing for the parishes, that a key earlier ruling stands for the idea that “you can’t treat religious institutions differently.”
“That’s not the principle that’s at issue here,” Kagan said. “The principle at issue here is: Do you have to treat them better?”
Chief Justice John Roberts also doubted that the court’s past wins for religious schools fit this case. “The law in those cases, in each of them, expressly discriminated against religious schools on its face,” Roberts told Reaves. “That’s not the case here.”
“The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation,” Reaves told the justices. “To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the Church’s teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the state has denied Colorado families the ability to use universal preschool funding at Catholic schools.”
The archdiocese runs 34 preschools, and its policy asks families to back church teaching on same-sex relationships and gender identity, Reuters reported. The wire service noted the catechism says “homosexual acts are intrinsically disordered.” (That’s the catechism’s wording, not Gayety’s.)
Dan and Lisa Sheley, Catholic parents, sued alongside the parishes in 2023. They say they’ve lost more than $12,000 in pre-K funding, Gayety reported last week. Enrollment at archdiocese preschools is down 20% since the program began, and two have closed, Becket says.
Reaves noted Colorado lets schools put low-income kids and kids with disabilities first. “Colorado has flexibly interpreted the mandate to accommodate important secular interests,” he said. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson told him that “it seems to me you’re asking for a special rule for religious schools,” one letting them skip Colorado’s condition that anyone taking the money be open to everyone.
Who Argued St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy
Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general, split time with Reaves on the parishes’ side, the court’s docket shows.
Helen Norton, Colorado’s deputy solicitor general, told the justices the program is “neutral towards religion.”
“Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage, free to teach them while receiving public funding,” Norton said.
Two Moms, Two Dads and Colorado’s Equal Opportunity Rule
Schools in the program sign an agreement to give kids “an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services” regardless of sexual orientation, gender identity and other traits, SCOTUSblog’s Amy Howe reported. GLAD Law and Lambda Legal backed the state in a brief. “A four-year-old shouldn’t lose their spot in preschool because of who their parents are,” GLAD Law’s case page says.
“Public funding carries public responsibility, and that basic contract cannot be selectively applied,” Mardi Moore, CEO of Rocky Mountain Equality, said in April, when the court took the case, Colorado Newsline reported.
10th Circuit Backed Colorado’s Pre-K Program in 2025
Colorado voters created the program with a 2020 ballot measure, and the parishes sued in 2023. After a January 2024 bench trial, a federal judge in Denver upheld the rule on sexual orientation and gender identity. The parishes won a narrower religious affiliation point, and the state then dropped its preference for church members, the 10th Circuit’s opinion says.
The appeals court affirmed on Sept. 30, 2025. “The nondiscrimination requirement exists in harmony with the First Amendment,” Judge Richard Federico wrote for a three-judge panel.
Supreme Court Ruling in Catholic Preschool Case Expected by June
Colorado leans on Employment Division v. Smith, the 1990 ruling that upheld “generally applicable” laws even when they burden religious practice, Reuters reported. On Tuesday, the conservatives seemed open to reading the Free Exercise Clause to cover some laws that burden religious groups in effect, along with laws that single them out, the wire service reported.
Republican-led states backing the parishes warned that siding with Colorado could let states “weaponize the same tactic against any religious organization that receives government funding for any public benefit program,” MS NOW reported.
The court has not ruled. Becket expects a decision by the end of June 2027.
